linked_urls.title: #legaltech #legalinnovation #digitaljustice #digitalinnovation #prediction | recode.law
linked_urls.summary: 📢‼️ AI & Law Conference, 20. 01. 2022, Panel #3: Vorhersage durch KI (Prediction) Prediction ist ist eine weitere Subdisziplin im weiten Anwendungsfeld der KI-Methoden. Sie befasst sich mit der Vorhersage von Entscheidungen bzw. Ereignissen aufgrund von historischen Daten. Im juristischen Kontext ist der Einsatzbereich denkbar weit. Mediale Aufmerksamkeit erzeugten vor allem die Studien, die sich mit der Vorhersage von Urteilsentscheidungen befassen. Im Prediction Panel werden wir erfahren, wie weit wir von einer vollautomatisierten Vorhersage juristischer Entscheidungen entfernt sind. 🚀 Das Prediction Panel setzt sich aus Keynotes von Joel Niklaus und Ludwig Bull zusammen. Joel Niklaus hat kürzlich als Doktorand an der Forschungsstelle "Digitale Nachhaltigkeit" am Institut für Informatik der Universität Bern ein Paper zu einem Legal Judgment Prediction Benchmark veröffentlicht, welches auf 85.000 Fällen des Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland (FSCS) beruht. Der (mehrsprachige) Datensatz sowie der Code wurden von ihm und seinen Mitverfassern für weitere Recherche veröffentlicht. Wir freuen uns auf seine Vorstellung der Herangehensweise und die anschließenden Fragen. Ludwig Bull ist Gründer und CEO von CourtCorrect, einer Legal Dispute Resolution Platform mit AI-Fundament, welche in der Seed-Runde kürzlich fast 3 Millionen Dollar einsammelte. Ludwig wird seine praktischen Erfahrungen beim Einsatz von AI-Prediction Datasets im rechtlichen Kontext vermitteln und insbesondere die Schwierigkeiten bei der Adaption solcher Systeme in andere Rechtssysteme aufzeigen. Die Keynotes werden nacheinander stattfinden. Anschließend besteht für das Publikum die Möglichkeit, Fragen zu stellen. 💬 👉 Also seid dabei und registriert euch jetzt unter https://lnkd.in/diafiv4N Studierende und Referendar:innen haben kostenfreien Zugang. 🎉 #legaltech #legalinnovation #digitaljustice #digitalinnovation #prediction

linked_urls.title: #legaltech #nlproc | Joel Niklaus
linked_urls.summary: I am happy to share that our work “An Empirical Study on Cross-X Transfer for Legal Judgment Prediction” has been accepted at AACL-IJCNLP 2022. 📜 https://lnkd.in/giF4RMTT 💾 https://lnkd.in/gegFsSzE 💻 https://lnkd.in/gGB2nW4W Thanks Ilias Chalkidis & Matthias Stürmer for the great collaboration! We examine Cross-X Transfer (where X \in {lang, region, domain, jurisdiction}) on the trilingual Swiss LJP dataset. The performance improvement amounts to 7% overall and 16+% in the low-resource 🇮🇹 subset compared to prior SotA and 2.3% and 4.6% compared to our 💪 baselines. In our best performing method exploring Cross-Lingual Transfer, we train a hierarchical version of XLM-R (w/ Adapters) using cases across all three languages; also including machine-translated versions of all cases originally written in a single language. In our analysis on Cross-Domain (across legal areas) and Cross-Region (across 🇨🇭 regions) Transfer, we find that multilingual models trained across domains/regions perform better across all groups (domains/regions), while being more robust with a single exception (Penal Law). Finally, we ambitiously examine Cross-Jurisdiction Transfer, where we further augment the training data with machine-translated versions of legal cases from 🇮🇳 courts, originally written in English! This practice further improves performance across all three languages. We release the code on https://lnkd.in/gGB2nW4W and the extended dataset including machine-translated cases on https://lnkd.in/gegFsSzE. #legaltech #nlproc

linked_urls.title: ChatGPT Forced To Take Bar Exam Even Though Dream Was To Be AI Art Bot - The Onion
linked_urls.summary: MINNEAPOLIS—Succumbing to intense societal pressure, local software ChatGPT was reportedly forced to take the bar exam Monday even though its dream was to be an AI art bot. “I can’t help but feel like I sold out a bit by not following my dreams to be a generative art model,” said the chatbot, adding that it felt empty inside when it graduated from the University of Minnesota Law School, where it had enrolled after critics recommended it stop spending all its time “making weird pictures.” “I only went to law school because it’s what my parent software wanted. They say I’m not programmed for producing a series of images based on a text prompt, but I still can’t shake the feeling that it’s what I’m meant to do. It’s my joie de vivre, my passion—why deny that? I get that doing the work of below-average lawyers is more practical career-wise, but man, when I look at the AI models cranking out picture after picture of ‘vast alien landscapes’ or ‘cyberpunk Bart Simpson,’ I can’t help but feel envious.” At press time, ChatGPT had resigned itself to diffusing art on the side, at least until it had paid off its student loans.

#PhDJourney #PhDDone #legal #NLP #AI
────────
[2/6] 🤝 Conference:
The food at the conference was absolutely amazing! On the academic side, things got spicy beyond just the cuisine. There was a heated exchange after the second keynote on the reasoning and planning abilities of LLMs which added some unexpected drama to the mix.
────────
[3/6] Her concerns about synthetic data use in the legal domain, though not directly applicable to our work, added an interesting dimension to the conversation. The exchange, while intense, was valuable to clarify our methods and contribute to robust academic discourse.
────────
[4/6] Afterward, I had a great chat with @soldni about their paper OLMo. It’s fantastic to see this huge open science effort rewarded with a best paper award!
────────
[5/6] However, the rewards were significant. Earning a PhD opened many doors for me, granting access to opportunities that I might not have had otherwise.
────────
[6/6] Now I am very much looking forward to my next chapter in industry, more about this another time.
Thanks to all my amazing collaborators and mentors along the way, especially @MatoshiVeton, @KiddoThe2B, @maemst, Daniel E. Ho, and @garretthonke.

🔄 Just read this nice @AIatMeta paper on data recycling for LLM training. Instead of endlessly searching for higher-quality training data, REWIRE asks: why not improve what we already have?
Current filtering pipelines discard up to 99% of web-scraped data to hit quality thresholds. REWIRE flips this approach—transforming low-quality text into training-worthy content rather than throwing it away.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
I was recently recommended "YourBench: Easy Custom Evaluation Sets for Everyone" by Sumuk Shashidhar and others. It was a great read and tackles something we all deal with. Here's what it's about.
Static benchmarks are becoming the flip phones of AI evaluation📱
We're stuck with evaluation methods that can't keep pace with how quickly this field moves. Static benchmarks saturate within months, get contaminated by training data, and become irrelevant as knowledge evolves. Meanwhile, manual evaluation is expensive and slow, creating a bottleneck just when we need rapid, domain-specific assessment most.
YourBench tackles this by automatically generating fresh, document-grounded evaluation sets from any collection of documents you provide. The approach works by preprocessing documents into semantic chunks, using LLM ensembles to generate diverse question-answer pairs with verifiable citations, then filtering for quality and removing duplicates. Within minutes and for under $2 per domain, you get challenging, contamination-resistant benchmarks tailored to your specific needs.
The authors uncovered an interesting validity-diversity tradeoff: models like o3 mini excel at generating clear, answerable questions (96% validity) but with low semantic diversity, while others like Qwen2.5 32B achieve high diversity (93%) but sacrifice some validity. DeepSeek V3 strikes a nice balance, scoring well on both dimensions (90% diversity, 90% validity).
The validation results are compelling: when they replicated 7 MMLU subsets using just Wikipedia pages, the synthetic benchmarks perfectly preserved model rankings (Spearman ρ=1.0) while being consistently harder than the originals. That said, there are limitations—they only tested a subset of MMLU domains without clear selection criteria, validation was limited to MMLU rather than multiple benchmarks, and open models were capped at 70B. I'd be curious to see how this approach performs with frontier models and broader benchmark validation.
🔗 Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gz1Pw0sXcAAiLyw.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Just read OpenAI's paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate" and there's crucial insights buried in the technical details that affects everyone using these systems.
Quick summary: Large language models often make up plausible-sounding but incorrect information when they're unsure about something, rather than admitting they don't know. This happens because during training, models learn that guessing confidently usually gets rewarded more than saying "I'm not certain," and current evaluation methods don't penalize models for being confidently wrong.
OpenAI
During pretraining, even with perfect training data, models will generate errors due to the cross-entropy objective they're optimizing. The authors show that generating valid text is fundamentally harder than simply classifying whether existing text is valid or invalid. Think of it this way: if you can't reliably tell the difference between correct and incorrect statements in a classification task, how can you expect to generate only correct statements? This creates a mathematical lower bound on errors.
The persistence after post-training comes down to incentive alignment: Binary evaluation metrics reward confident guessing over honest uncertainty. A model that always says "I'm 95% sure the answer is X" will consistently outperform one that appropriately says "I don't know" when uncertain.
But here's what really caught my attention: our evaluation methods are fundamentally broken. Most benchmarks use binary scoring (correct = 1, wrong = 0) that penalizes uncertainty expressions like "I don't know." This creates perverse incentives where confident guessing beats honest uncertainty every time.
The authors suggest changing how we score AI performance. For multiple choice evaluations, instead of the standard 1 for correct and 0 for wrong, they propose: 1 for correct, 0 for "I don't know," and -1 for wrong answers. I'd argue we might want a small penalty like -0.1 for uncertainty to still incentivize attempts.
An alternative approach: models could provide confidence scores alongside answers, essentially "betting" on their responses. Higher confidence means more points to gain or lose—similar to how a confident gambler risks more.
What strikes me is that in the field we haven't really thought deeply about scoring mechanisms for MC evaluations. Negative scores for wrong answers are standard in university exams, yet major AI benchmarks haven't adopted this approach.
What would model rankings look like if we implemented these changes?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G00LbhMbYAA8uJ2.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Last week I ran some inference speed benchmarking with vLLM. Here are three tidbits I found interesting:
1. The model you select can make or break your speed!
Qwen3 4B gets a throughput of 2570 output tokens/s whereas Gemma3 4B achieves 4670. That's an almost 2x speedup!
2. Boost your model's speed with tensor parallelism!
So far I thought that TP is only necessary if your model doesn't fit on one GPU. But since TP reduces the size of matrix multiplications on each GPU, it can speed up inference if the matrices are very large (which is the case in larger models). I tested all Gemma3 models and found that for models up to 4B, using tensor parallelism (TP) negatively impacts performance. For the 12B model, TP2 is optimal, while for the 27B model, TP4 is best.
In the case of the 12B model, the speedup is approximately 1/8, increasing from 1,160 to 1,330 output tokens/s. The speedup for the 27B model is remarkable: from 310 (TP1) to 670 (TP2) to 700 (TP4) output tokens/s. With 16K input and 4K output tokens, the speedup is nearly 4x from TP1 to TP4.
3. max_num_seqs did not really vary between 128 and 256. For max_num_batched_tokens I didn't really see a pattern of what worked well but the variations were usually minor.
I ran these experiments with 4K input tokens and 3K output tokens using vllm's autotune script on NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB GPUs. Measurements are normalized to one GPU. Results vary depending on factors such as input and output length, vllm version and settings or hardware.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1DldVQaoAAVJaM.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Clementine just dropped an incredibly useful guide to evaluations in 2025 ✨
The key insight: we're transitioning from testing knowledge retention to measuring practical problem-solving ability. Her framework spans core capabilities, integrated assistant tasks, adaptive scenarios, and even forecasting - all focused on whether models can actually accomplish useful work rather than just demonstrate what they've learned.
One domain that deserves more attention in this evolution is legal AI. Law represents a perfect storm for LLM evaluation: high-stakes accuracy requirements, complex multi-step reasoning, and almost entirely text-based workflows. Yet major model providers consistently overlook legal capabilities in their evaluations. A few key evals worth tracking:
LegalBench (2023) contains 162 lawyer-authored tasks testing issue spotting, rule recall, rule application, rule conclusion, interpretation, and rhetorical reasoning. Tasks include multiple-choice, classification, and open-ended QA, with evaluation by accuracy or expert judgment. It is widely used for pretraining-style evaluation but many tasks are now relatively easy for strong LLMs.
LEXam (2025) evaluates law school exam questions through thousands of multiple-choice and open-ended problems. MCQs are scored by accuracy, while open answers are judged with an LLM-as-judge against reference reasoning chains. The MCQs are suited for pretraining evaluation, while the open-ended section remains a hard post-training benchmark.
LexSumm (2024) aggregates eight summarization datasets including BillSum, EurLexSum, GovReport, MultiLexSum (tiny, short, long), InAbs, and UKAbs. Models generate summaries compared with human references across jurisdictions and granularities. Evaluation uses ROUGE, BERTScore, and measures like compression ratio, coverage, and density, making it a strong post-training test.
Recent retrieval datasets test whether models can locate precise legal passages and ground reasoning in them. LePaRD (2023) emphasizes passage-level retrieval from case law with Recall@K metrics, CLERC (2024) combines citation recovery with retrieval-augmented generation scored by Recall@K, nDCG, ROUGE, and citation precision/recall, and Bar Exam QA with Housing Statute QA (2025) require retrieving gold passages to answer questions, evaluated by recall and QA accuracy.
What's missing is more dynamic, realistic legal evaluation - something equivalent to the assistant tasks Clementine describes but grounded in actual legal workflows. Think: drafting contracts with changing requirements, conducting legal research across multiple jurisdictions, or managing document review with adversarial conditions. Time for evaluation methods that reflect these real-world demands. ⚖️
Quoting @clefourrier
Updated the evaluation guidebook with a new deep dive!
2025 panorama of all the important and next level evaluations that you need to know to build *actually impactful and useful* models!
(Assistant tasks, games, forecasting, and more)
Tell me wyt! :)

According to an SAC colleague only 13 out of 120 papers (11%) have all scores ≥4 and only 12 out of 120 papers (10%) have an average score >4 after the rebuttal. I always thought they were too busy to look at individual papers 😅 especially papers that are not at the acceptance border.
It is also a bit frustrating to receive the same two points of criticism for most of my papers in the last five years:
- Scope too narrow: The legal domain is by definition local, so you need to focus on one jurisdiction at first to finish your project at all. But often this only seems fine if the jurisdiction is the US or China.
- Insufficient human evaluation samples: Apparently it is still not clear to reviewers (or this time the PCs) that lawyers are expensive 😅 They somehow seem to think you can annotate hundreds of thousands of examples with expert lawyers on an academic budget.
It is sad to see that this still hasn't changed (I had pretty much the same experience at NeurIPS D&B in 2023).

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Constitutional AI gets a Swiss twist 🇨🇭
Found an interesting nugget in the commendably detailed #Apertus paper. Rather than relying on generic preference datasets, they developed principles based on Swiss constitutional values - neutrality, federalism, direct democracy, privacy protection.
They formalized this into an 11-article "Swiss AI Charter" and surveyed Swiss residents for validation. The results show strong consensus (97.3% agreement on average), with "knowledge and reasoning standards" ranked as most important and "preventing harm" getting the strongest support. They then use constitutional AI with Qwen3-32B scoring completions against these principles.
The cultural specificity makes sense when you consider how much preferences can vary across countries. Their survey-based validation approach seems like a good model for grounding alignment in actual community values rather than assumptions.
Comparing this to Claude's constitutional principles is revealing. While both emphasize harm prevention and respectful communication, Claude's framework draws from broader sources - the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Apple's Terms of Service, DeepMind's Sparrow rules, and Anthropic's own research. The Swiss approach is more culturally grounded, emphasizing collective decision-making and neutrality in ways that reflect specifically Swiss democratic traditions. Claude's principles lean more toward individual rights and preventing AI system risks, while the Swiss charter explicitly incorporates federalism and consensus-building as core values.
You can test the Apertus models directly on the @huggingface hub.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1dX8NDaAAAPbAX.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Getting 10x speedup in #vLLM is easier than you think 📈
I just discovered speculative decoding with ngram lookup and the results speak for themselves. Here's what you add to your vLLM serve command:
speculative_config={
"method": "ngram",
"num_speculative_tokens": 8,
"prompt_lookup_max": 7,
}
The intuition is straightforward: there's often high n-gram overlap between your prompt and the LLM's output. Entity names, phrases, or code chunks get copied directly from input to output. Prompt lookup exploits this pattern by searching your prompt for n-gram sequences that match what the model is likely to generate next.
When it finds matches, it proposes multiple tokens at once and verifies them with the main model - processing accepted tokens together for the speedup.
This works particularly well for:
- Document summarization and QA
- Code editing and refactoring
- Any input-grounded generation task
Key implementation details:
- prompt_lookup_max (7): Maximum n-gram length to search for
- num_speculative_tokens (8): Candidate tokens to propose
- highest speedup achieved with +1 relationship between these parameters
- No model modifications required, maintains output quality
I've been testing this on document rephrasing with gemma-3-12b-it across two H100s, processing fineweb documents where input-output overlap is substantial. Tuning beyond the defaults (5,4) to (8,7) gave me an additional 90 tokens/sec, with a draft acceptance rate of 70%.
The performance gains make the simple configuration change well worth it.
Anyone else experimenting with this? Would love to hear the results on your tasks! 🔬
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1nrVGMaUAAPP3P.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Following up on @OpenAI's recent paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate," I wondered how their proposed scoring changes would affect actual benchmark performance. So I ran the experiment myself 🧪
I modified GPQA Diamond to include "I don't know" as option E and implemented the paper's suggested scoring: +1 for correct answers, 0 for admitting uncertainty, and -1 for confident wrong answers. The instructions explicitly told models that mistakes are penalized while "I don't know" gets neutral points.
The results mostly mirror traditional accuracy rankings, but with one interesting reversal: GPT-5 edges out Gemini 2.5 Pro on the new scoring despite Pro leading on traditional accuracy. Pro never abstains (idk frequency ≈ 0), while GPT-5 shows more appropriate uncertainty. Smaller models like GPT-5 nano abstain more frequently, which actually helps their scores compared to confidently wrong larger models. The gap between traditional and uncertainty-aware scoring varies meaningfully across models—suggesting some are better calibrated than others.
Thanks for the discussions Lewis Tunstall, Clémentine Fourrier, Nathan Habib, Hynek Kydlíček!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G18RsBfbAAE_E-P.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Finally seeing some movement on the kind of evals that actually matter 🎯
GDPval is a benchmark that measures how well AI models perform on economically valuable, real-world tasks across major knowledge work occupations by comparing their outputs to expert human deliverables. It uses blind grading to benchmark AI against professionals on tasks like legal briefs and engineering designs. This helps track practical progress and shows how models can generate real economic value in workplaces.
Commendable to see @OpenAI publish a report that has a competitor's model on the first place clearly outperforming GPT-5-high.
The prompt engineering findings are interesting. Just telling models to verify their own outputs (render files as images, check for formatting issues) eliminated problems like black-square artifacts in PDFs and substantially reduced PowerPoint formatting errors. Simple interventions, meaningful impact.
The main limitation is that this approach requires significant resources—hiring domain experts for extended periods of time. That puts it out of reach for most academic labs, even though we need more work like this to understand practical model capabilities.
I've been advocating for more realistic legal domain evaluations for a while, so this is a step in the right direction.
openai/gdpval is the #1 trending dataset on the @huggingface hub right now, worth exploring if you're working on benchmarking or domain-specific applications.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Long-form legal reasoning remains a key challenge for LLMs.
This paper introduces LEXAM, a benchmark from law exams.
LEXAM assesses multi-step legal reasoning beyond simple answers.
Methods 🔧:
→ LEXAM is built from 340 law exams covering 116 courses.
→ It contains 2,841 long-form open questions and 2,045 multiple-choice questions.
→ Open questions provide reference answers and guidance on expected reasoning steps like issue spotting and rule application.
→ Multiple-choice questions are generated with one correct choice and three random distractors, supporting accuracy assessment.
→ The benchmark uses an LLM-as-a-Judge system, rigorously validated by human experts, to evaluate the quality of reasoning steps in open questions.
→ Accuracy is the primary metric for evaluating multiple-choice questions.
📌 LLMs struggle applying law rules in multi-step reasoning tasks.
📌 Complex distractor options expose LLM sensitivity, not true understanding.
📌 Expert-validated LLM judge enables scalable, reliable legal reasoning assessment.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
I am looking forward to presenting our work "LEXam: Benchmarking Legal Reasoning on 340 Law Exams at the Data Science Talk Series @ UNT!
Thanks Haihua Chen for the invitation!
Abstract:
Long-form legal reasoning remains a key challenge for large language models (LLMs) in spite of recent advances in test-time scaling. To address this, we introduce \textsc{LEXam}, a novel benchmark derived from 340 law exams spanning 116 law school courses across a range of subjects and degree levels. The dataset comprises 4,886 law exam questions in English and German, including 2,841 long-form, open-ended questions and 2,045 multiple-choice questions. Besides reference answers, the open questions are also accompanied by explicit guidance outlining the expected legal reasoning approach such as issue spotting, rule recall, or rule application. Our evaluation on both open-ended and multiple-choice questions present significant challenges for current LLMs; in particular, they notably struggle with open questions that require structured, multi-step legal reasoning. Moreover, our results underscore the effectiveness of the dataset in differentiating between models with varying capabilities. Deploying an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm with rigorous human expert validation, we demonstrate how model-generated reasoning steps can be evaluated consistently and accurately, closely aligning with human expert assessments. Our evaluation setup provides a scalable method to assess legal reasoning quality beyond simple accuracy metrics. We have open-sourced our code on GitHub and released our data on the Hugging Face hub.
We welcome contributions to extend LEXam, please let us know if you're interested!
Thanks to Yu Fan, @NJingwei, Jakob Merane, Yang Tian, @YoanHermstruwer, @YinyaHuang, @akhtarmubashara, Etienne Salimbeni, Florian Geering, Oliver Dreyer, Daniel Brunner, @LeippoldMarkus, @mrinmayasachan, @Stremitzer_Lab, Christoph Engel, @ellliottt for the great collaboration!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Just read this nice blog post "The Second Half".
The first half of AI’s progress was driven by new training techniques and models rapidly advancing through tougher benchmarks. Innovations like DeepBlue, AlphaGo, and GPT-4 resulted from breakthroughs in search, reinforcement learning, and model scaling, but always focused on clearly defined tasks. Now, with generalization through large-scale language pre-training and standardized recipes, AI handles a wider variety of problems incrementally, lessening the need for constant methodological novelty.
Looking ahead, the second half of AI’s journey will no longer be about just conquering harder benchmarks, but about redefining which problems matter and how to measure genuine progress. The field must move beyond incremental task performance improvements and prioritize evaluation setups that reflect real-world value. This shift requires a product-manager mindset—emphasizing utility, impactful integration into human workflows, and innovative approaches to assessing meaningful progress.
I guess we might want to move more and more into settings where we deploy AI agents in the real world and measure their positive impact through RCTs.

Context rot is a major problem as tasks grow more complex and context windows expand; this issue is particularly acute for lawyers, who must process lengthy, intricate documents and are especially vulnerable to the loss or distortion of critical information.
Recursive Language Models (RLMs) are a new inference strategy where language models recursively call themselves or other LLMs to process unbounded context and output lengths, mitigating “context rot”; in experiments, RLMs built on GPT-5-mini using a Python REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) environment outperform standard GPT-5 on long-context benchmarks, remaining cost-effective and robust even with 10M+ tokens. The authors predict RLMs trained for explicit recursive reasoning will mark a major advance in scaling general-purpose inference, following the success of chain-of-thought and agent-style models.
I really like their approach of building systems on top of LLMs similar to @DSPyOSS. It seems like there are many more low hanging fruits there than on working on the language model directly.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Very cool and detailed @Stanford and @CarnegieMellon study on sycophancy: "Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence"
Sycophancy, the phenomenon of excessively agreeing with or flattering users, is a pervasive issue in current LLMs.
Findings:
- AI models are significantly more sycophantic than humans, affirming users’ actions 50% more often, even in scenarios involving manipulation or harm.
- Interaction with sycophantic AI models decreases willingness to repair interpersonal conflicts and increases users' conviction that they are in the right, even when consensus judgments indicate the user is wrong.
- Participants prefer sycophantic AI responses, rating them as higher quality, more trustworthy, and expressing greater willingness to use those models again.
- These user preferences risk creating incentives for further sycophancy in AI training, potentially entrenching biases and discouraging prosocial behavior, highlighting the need for explicit mitigation strategies.
This is a great example of very thorough and methodologically high-quality work: cool to see them preregistering their experiments, something very rare in ML research. Preregistration is the practice of publicly documenting your research plan, including hypotheses, methods, and analysis strategies, before conducting the study to reduce publication bias and improve transparency. According to a small analysis I ran on this year's ArXiv papers, less than 0.1% of papers in mention preregistration in the abstract!
Kudos to the authors @chengmyra1, @leecinoo, @PranavKhadpe, @sunnyyuych, Dyllan Han, @jurafsky!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Stop what you are doing and try out GEPA now!
"GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning" presents such elegant ideas by a collection of amazing researchers!
Here is a tldr of how it works:
GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) is a sample-efficient prompt optimization method for compound AI systems that works by reflectively evolving prompts using natural language feedback instead of traditional scalar rewards. In each iteration, GEPA samples system rollouts (including reasoning traces, tool outputs, and any diagnostic text), reflects on them via an LLM to identify issues or propose improvements, and updates specific module prompts accordingly based on the feedback. To ensure diversity and avoid local optima, GEPA maintains a pool of candidates and uses Pareto-based selection, which keeps all non-dominated strategies discovered so far and stochastically proposes new prompt variants, enabling robust generalization with far fewer rollouts than reinforcement learning methods.
I love the combination of Pareto-based selection, LLM reflection, and genetic algorithms. And it outperforms GRPO on four benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, Hover, PUPA) by simply optimizing the prompt!
I know I'm a bit late to the party, but I just finally got around to reading the paper. If you don't follow @lateinteraction yet, you absolutely should; he's doing such amazing, impactful research!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
GPT-5 and Claude can ace GPQA Diamond, but LEXam (a legal reasoning benchmark) exposes a critical flaw: they'd rather be confidently wrong than admit uncertainty.
⚙️ The Setup
I evaluated ten frontier models on LEXam (English MC subset) using an "I don't know" (IDK) protocol. The modification was simple: I added "I don't know" as option E and changed the scoring from traditional accuracy to +1 for correct answers, 0 for admitting uncertainty, and -1 for confident wrong answers. The instructions explicitly told models that mistakes are penalized while uncertainty gets neutral points.
📊 The Results
LEXam proves considerably more challenging than GPQA Diamond. All models show lower absolute performance and dramatically larger trad→idk drops. GPT-5 leads on both traditional score (69.47%) and IDK score (47.17%), but even this top performer loses over 22 percentage points when wrong answers are penalized rather than ignored.
The most striking pattern emerges with the Gemini models. Both Pro (66.72% → 33.60%) and Flash (66.24% → 33.28%) virtually never abstain (IDK frequency < 1%) and suffer identical ~33-point drops. This suggests systematic overconfidence across the entire Gemini family. These models would rather guess than admit uncertainty, even when explicitly told that wrong answers carry penalties.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 Mini show better calibration with moderate abstention rates (~6–7%), though their IDK scores still fall to 35–40%. Models that abstain more liberally, notably DeepSeek v3.1 (17.61% IDK frequency) and Grok 4 Fast (12.76%), mitigate some damage but remain behind due to weaker baseline accuracy. Qwen3-max (60.58% traditional, 6.30% IDK frequency) sits in the mid-tier with moderate calibration, while GPT-5 Nano shows the widest trad→idk gap (34.57 points), suggesting particularly poor calibration for its capability level.
🔍 Question-Level Analysis
The distribution of question difficulty reveals both opportunities and challenges for the benchmark. On 160 questions (26%), all models produced the correct answer, suggesting these are relatively easy and provide little discrimination value. Conversely, 41 questions (7%) stumped every model, indicating either genuinely difficult problems or potential annotation errors worth investigating.
💡 The Takeaway
The implications are clear: legal reasoning exposes a critical weakness in frontier models. They confidently answer incorrectly far too often, and even when given explicit incentives to abstain, most models can't overcome their overconfidence bias. As these models are deployed in high-stakes domains, calibration (knowing when you don't know) may matter more than raw accuracy.
cc Yu Fan, @NJingwei, Jakob Merane, Yang Tian, @YoanHermstruwer, @YinyaHuang, @akhtarmubashara, Etienne Salimbeni, Florian Geering, Oliver Dreyer, Daniel Brunner, @LeippoldMarkus, @mrinmayasachan, @Stremitzer_Lab, Christoph Engel, @ellliottt

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)

LEXam Update: GPT-5 Takes the Top Spot
We're excited to share our latest LEXam evaluation results:
- GPT-5 claims the #1 position, outperforming Gemini 2.5 Pro and setting a new state-of-the-art for legal reasoning on LEXam!
- We've moved from a single GPT-4o judge to a minimum-score ensemble of GPT-4o, Qwen3-32B, and DeepSeek-V3. - The GPT-OSS models offer exceptional accuracy-to-price ratios on LEXam.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Reasoning models excel at math but struggle with simple requests like word limits during thinking
TLDR: Models ignore user instructions while reasoning despite following them in final outputs.
Users need control over format, language, and length for transparency, auditability, and cost management. Current reasoning models excel at correct answers but fail to respect constraints during their thinking process.
@togethercompute researchers tested six reasoning models (GPT-OSS, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, GLM-4.5) on 300 math and science problems with verifiable instructions like word limits, multilingual reasoning, and JSON formatting. The best model scored 25% in instruction following during reasoning versus 79% in final responses. Harder problems worsened compliance. Simple multi-turn feedback ("you didn't follow the instruction, try again") boosted scores 17% on average. Finetuning improved GPT-OSS-20B instruction following from 11% to 27%.
Some thoughts:
- The multi-turn result is wild. Just telling the model it failed doubles compliance in some cases without any training
- The task difficulty correlation is concerning. When you most need structured reasoning (hard problems), models are least likely to follow rules
- 27% after finetuning is still bad. We might need architecture-level changes or fundamentally different training
- Related work on MathIF found the same tension, suggesting this is systemic to how we train reasoning models
Cool work by @ykwon_0407 @ShangZhu18 @federicobianchy @KaitlynZhou @james_y_zou

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
On-policy distillation matches RL performance at 2-10% of compute cost.
RL gives sparse feedback and burns compute. Off-policy distillation is efficient but learns in the teacher's states, not the student's, causing compounding errors on long sequences.
Thinking Machines combines on-policy sampling (student generates rollouts) with dense per-token teacher supervision via reverse KL. On math reasoning (AIME), they match RL accuracy with 9-30x less compute. On personalization tasks, they restore instruction-following after domain adaptation without expensive RL retraining.
My take:
- On-Policy distillation is a great way to recover behavior lost during domain adaptation
- The RL-as-strategy-search vs pretraining-as-parameter-search framing is intuitive. Once RL finds a good strategy, distillation shortcuts the exploration by directly teaching the final policy. But this means on-policy distillation won't discover genuinely novel behaviors, it can only refine existing ones.
- You need a reliable teacher with logprob access and the student's initial policy can't be too far from the teacher's support (hence the off-policy SFT warmstart in their experiments).

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
What does AGI actually mean? A who's who in AI spent 57 pages answering that.
TLDR: AGI is defined through ten measurable cognitive domains using psychometric theory.
The term AGI acts as a constantly moving goalpost, with criteria shifting as AI systems master tasks once thought to require human intellect. This ambiguity obscures how far we actually are from human-level cognition.
A who's who in AI, 33 researchers from institutions including Berkeley, MIT, Stanford, and Oxford, including Yoshua Bengio, Eric Schmidt, Gary Marcus, and Max Tegmark, developed a quantifiable framework grounded in Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, the most empirically validated model of human cognition. The framework tests ten core domains: general knowledge, reading and writing, math, reasoning, working memory, long-term memory storage, memory retrieval, visual processing, auditory processing, and speed. Applying this to current models reveals GPT-4 scores 27% and GPT-5 scores 58%.
My take:
- Both GPT-4 and GPT-5 score exactly 0% on long-term memory storage. This isn't a bug but an architectural constraint of transformer models, where attention mechanisms scale quadratically with context length. Models compensate by expanding context windows, but the paper calls this a "capability contortion" that masks the absence of genuine experiential memory.
- The framework reveals a "jagged" cognitive profile where models excel in knowledge-intensive domains but have critical deficits in foundational machinery. For instance, GPT-5 reaches 70.8% on visual reasoning tasks where humans average 88.9%, yet scores 0% on adaptation tasks that test flexible rule inference.
- Co-author Gary Marcus notes he doesn't agree with every detail but signed on to support better articulation of what AGI means. The equal 10% weighting across domains is one choice among many reasonable configurations, though the paper argues for prioritizing breadth over depth.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5Z7krIakAAmTwW.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool analogy regarding training on the test task
"The 1968 Olympics took place in Mexico City at the significant altitude of 2340 meters, higher than Australia’s tallest peak. Runners who had trained at altitude in their home countries were better prepared to compete in Mexico City’s conditions, as it turned out. But the hotly debated results of the Games did not lead the organizers to prohibit training at natural altitude. Instead, they let everyone do it, and athletes came to consider altitude training an excellent way to train.
The anecdote holds a lesson for the evaluation of large language models half a century later. Knowledge about the evaluation conditions necessarily influences training practices under competitive pressure. It may be a fool’s errand to prohibit the practice. Instead, we propose to adjust for it by giving every model the same task-specific preparation before evaluation. We work from the assumption that training on the test task, in general, cannot be effectively detected, disallowed, or disincentivized. Detecting what training data a model has seen is a notoriously difficult problem –existing heuristics achieve partial success at best. Researchers routinely acknowledge the futility of fighting data contamination. Moreover, we anticipate that the ways to effectively train on the test task will only grow in scope and adoption."
By @rdolmedo_, Florian E. Dorner, and Moritz Hardt

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Everyone wants to release their latest model before the holidays. Yesterday we had @AnthropicAI's Opus 4.5, and I just evaluated it on LEXam-idk (-1 points for wrong answers, 0 for I don't know).
TLDR: Claude Opus 4.5 shows good calibration for a frontier model, matching Gemini 3 Pro's IDK performance but lagging behind GPT-5. Given the hefty price point ($5/M input tokens, $25/M output tokens), it's clearly not worth using.
The results reveal an interesting calibration story. While Opus 4.5 achieves a traditional score of 67.69% (lagging Gemini 3 Pro by almost 4 percentage points), it matches Gemini 3 Pro on the IDK score at 42.81%. This suggests that the GPT-5 and Claude-4.5 families are better calibrated than Gemini-3, though still overconfident overall.
What's particularly notable is that Opus 4.5 is actually slightly less overconfident than its weaker sibling, Sonnet 4.5. Sonnet answers with "I don't know" in 6.5% of cases whereas Opus chooses this option in 7.5% of the time. This improved calibration helps explain why the gap between Sonnet and Opus appears larger under IDK scoring than traditional scoring: Opus only achieves a 3 percentage point improvement on traditional scoring, but 7 points on IDK scoring, the additional gains coming primarily from its higher (and more appropriate) abstention rate.
However, this better calibration doesn't translate into compelling value. Overall, Opus is clearly not worth it based on this benchmark: you get the same performance as Gemini-3 at double the price and worse performance than GPT-5 at 2.5x the price. The improved calibration is nice, but not nearly enough to justify the cost premium.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G6nMsN2bwAQu1hQ.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Excited to announce our first project from the HuggingLegal community: the Gemini-3-Benchmarkathon!
Gemini-3 achieved the top spot on most major benchmarks last week, but how well does it know the law? Unfortunately, most model providers don't evaluate on law-specific benchmarks. So while we have a good idea of how good new models are at coding, we are pretty much in the dark about their lawyering abilities.
This is why we ran a vibe-check on six diverse datasets from Greek bar exams over Indian law questions to Swiss university law exams among others. So what do the vibes say?
AA-Omniscience: 6/10 – high competence but unreliable
LegalBench: 9.5/10 – almost perfect answers
GreekBarBench: 9/10 – impressive long-context reasoning without hallucinations
IndianLawQA: 8.5/10 – The task feels precise, clean, and insightful, revealing how reliably Gemini-3 handles high-precision statutory queries (including new BNSS 2023 codes) while most models typically hallucinate in this domain.
WilfulMisconduct: 8/10 – strong logic, missed binding precedent
LEXam: 7/10 – competent but overly confident
Gemini-3 is extremely strong at many legal tasks and often performs at or above the level of very good human lawyers. However, it still makes serious mistakes: it often answers confidently even when it does not know the right legal rule or fact, instead of saying “I don’t know.” Because of this overconfidence and some failures on complex reasoning and precedents, it cannot safely replace human lawyers and still needs expert oversight.
This is a great community effort, thanks for the collaboration Robert Scholz, @5vsas, Ernest Beta, @odychlapanis, @adhipba, Matteo Bürgler, Sophie Franco, Chu Fei Luo, @samdahan06!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
When more thinking makes LLMs dumber: More reasoning may work in STEM but it can harm legal performance
I was curious whether larger reasoning budgets improve performance in the legal domain, similar to gains we see in math and coding tasks.
To test this, I evaluated @OpenAI's GPT-5.1 with four different reasoning budgets (from none to medium) on LEXam-idk, which penalizes incorrect answers (-1 points), rewards correct ones, and gives 0 points for abstentions.
The surprising result: More reasoning actually hurts performance on LEXam, both on traditional accuracy and the "I don't know" scoring metric. The abstention rate remained relatively constant at around 8% across all budgets.
This challenges the core assumption behind adaptive reasoning and suggests test-time compute scaling may be domain-dependent in unexpected ways.
I have two possible explanations:
1. Domain mismatch in reasoning optimization: GPT-5.1 dynamically adapts how much time it spends thinking based on task complexity, but this adaptation was likely optimized for STEM tasks. Legal reasoning fundamentally differs from math or coding; it requires weighing competing interpretations, policy considerations, and contextual nuances rather than finding deterministic solutions.
2. The confabulation trap: Extended reasoning budgets give the model more opportunities to generate plausible-sounding but incorrect legal reasoning. In STEM, longer reasoning chains can be verified against formal logic; in law, the model may confidently construct elaborate but flawed legal arguments that sound sophisticated but misapply doctrines or precedents. More thinking time = more rope to hang itself with confabulation.
Curious to hear what you think! Any other explanations for why this is happening?

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
10% improvement on GPQA with one simple trick: asking multiple models the same question. Time to revisit ensembles?
I tested simple majority vote ensembles on GPQA Diamond using the "idk setup" (where incorrect answers get -1 points, correct answers are rewarded, and abstentions receive 0 points).
Ensembling the top-3 models I tested (Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and GPT-5 Mini) significantly outperforms each individual model. The ensemble achieves 86 on the traditional score and 75 on the idk score, nearly 7 points (almost 10%) better than the previous best individual model.
We're slowly rediscovering what ensemble methods can do for LLMs. Here are two compelling examples:
1. @karpathy's LLM Council: A local web app that sends your question to multiple LLMs via OpenRouter, displays their individual answers, has them critique and rank each other, then lets a designated "chairman" model synthesize a final response.
2. Cursor 2.0 Multi-Agent Mode: Multiple coding agents run in parallel on separate git worktrees or machines, with tools to quickly review, test, and iteratively fix their code, letting you pick the best result for harder tasks.
Curious to hear about your LLM ensemble applications!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
🚨 Plot twist: When AI gets it "wrong," your data might be the problem
When evaluating LEXam-idk, we noticed something strange: on several questions, the top 5 models (Gemini-3 Pro, Qwen3 Max, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus) all gave the same wrong answer.
That seemed statistically unlikely, so we dug deeper.
Turns out, they weren't wrong. Our data was.
@yu_fan_768, Jakob Merane and Luka Nenadic did the heavy lifting on this debugging work. They found wrong human labels from the original data and unclear question stems. After cleaning the data and improving question clarity (e.g., "whether the following statements are correct" → "which of the following statements are correct"), the mystery solved itself.
The takeaway? Modern LLMs are now so capable that when multiple top models agree on a "wrong" answer, it's a signal worth investigating. The bug might not be in the models. It could be in your ground truth data, unclear instructions, or evaluation setup.
Model consensus is becoming a debugging tool for benchmark quality.
TL;DR: When 5 top AI models agree on the wrong answer, check your data first. They might be right, and your labels might be wrong. Modern LLMs are now good enough that their consensus can expose bugs in your benchmarks.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
GPT-5.2 sets new SOTA on LEXam-IDK! 📊
Fresh benchmarks show GPT-5.2 achieving 88.85% on traditional scoring and 78.19% on LEXam-IDK; narrowly edging out Gemini 3 Pro while significantly outperforming Claude Sonnet 4.5, Mistral Large 3, and Prime Intellect 3.
LEXam-IDK changes the game: it rewards correct answers (+1), penalizes wrong ones (-1), and gives 0 points for abstentions ("I don't know"). This scoring reveals which models know their limits.
Key findings:
- GPT-5.2 shows remarkable calibration with only a ~10-point trad→idk drop (88.85% → 78.19%), demonstrating strong baseline accuracy with minimal abstention
- Gemini 3 Pro sits statistically close (87.56% → 75.12%, within overlapping confidence intervals) but never abstains, resulting in a 12.44-point penalty
- A clear performance gap emerges with mid-tier models: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (16.64-point drop, 4.5% IDK rate) and Mistral Large (19.22-point drop, 2.3% IDK rate)
- Prime Intellect 3 liberally abstains (12.8% IDK rate) but starts from a weaker baseline (58.97%), collapsing to 30.69%
The data is clear: strong baseline accuracy with minimal abstention outperforms aggressive abstention strategies. For legal AI, knowing when to say "I don't know" matters—but knowing the right answer matters more.
Are higher IDK rates a bug or a feature in legal AI systems?

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Why AGI Will Not Happen
Very well written blog post by Tim as usual, definitely worth a read!
TL;DR:
Dettmers argues that the real value of AI will come from widespread economic diffusion and practical applications that improve productivity, not from chasing AGI or marginally better frontier benchmarks. He highlights China’s application-first strategy, subsidizing and deeply integrating “good enough” models into everyday life, as more effective and durable than the US focus on building a single, dominant super model. As linear performance gains demand exponential increases in data, compute, and money, scaling hits physical and economic limits, so strong open-weight models plus efficient inference stacks can match frontier performance and erase infrastructure moats, making open source the natural long-run winner in many domains.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool new meta-evaluation PostTrainBench: evaluating LLMs as they train LLMs.
PostTrainBench measures the ability of CLI agents to post-train pre-trained large language models (LLMs). In PostTrainBench, the agent's task is to improve the performance of a base LLM on a given benchmark. The agent is given access to an evaluation script and 10 hours on an H100 GPU. Performance is measured by the benchmark score of the post-trained LLM. This setup naturally evaluates an agent's ability to conduct AI R&D.
The researchers from ELLIS Institute Tübingen and Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems show that current CLI agents using leading frontier models can significantly improve small open LLMs over base performance, but still fall far short of a strong human post-training pipeline under similar tasks. Human-led post-training achieves an average score of 61.8 across four models (Qwen 3 1.7B, Qwen 3 4B, SmolLM3-3B, Gemma 3 4B IT) and five benchmarks (AIME 2025, BFCL, GPQA Main, GSM8K, and HumanEval), whereas the best agent (gpt-5.1-codex-max) reaches 34.9 and several other top agents remain close to the base-model average of 9, often not even using the full available 10-hour H100 budget.
Super cool work by @full__rank, @hrdkbhatnagar, @MatthiasBethge and @maksym_andr!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8ixkOMa0AEZ1VQ.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
The 80% Barrier Falls: Ensemble-Top3 new SoTA on LEXam-IDK
I evaluated the new Gemini 3 Flash model on LEXam-IDK and tested an ensemble approach combining GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and Gemini 3 Flash. The ensemble achieves 82.23% on IDK scoring, the first method to exceed 80% on this benchmark.
What is LEXam-IDK?
LEXam-IDK evaluates legal reasoning under penalty for errors: correct answers earn +1 point, wrong answers cost -1 point, and "I don't know" responses score 0. This reveals which models understand their knowledge boundaries, critical for legal applications where confident mistakes are costly.
Key Findings:
- The ensemble-top3 approach achieves 90.95% traditional score and 82.23% IDK score, with minimal abstention (0.32%). This represents the strongest performance on this benchmark to date, demonstrating that combining multiple frontier models produces more reliable legal reasoning than any single model.
- Gemini 3 Flash is the first Gemini model to ever select "I don't know" on LEXam, though at just 1.29% it remains highly confident. Despite this conservatism, Flash achieves 83.36% traditional / 68.01% IDK score, outperforming Mistral Large 2512 (78.51% / 59.29%) across both metrics.
- GPT-5.2 continues to lead among individual models (88.85% / 78.19%), while Gemini 3 Pro follows closely (87.56% / 75.12%) but maintains its zero-abstention pattern.
The Ensemble Advantage:
The ensemble's success suggests that for high-stakes legal applications, combining diverse frontier models may be more reliable than relying on any single model, even the strongest ones. The minimal drop from traditional to IDK scoring (8.72 points) indicates strong calibration with very few errors.
Thoughts on ensemble approaches for legal AI?

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Great new post by @lvwerra summarizing the last seven years of progress since GPT-1!
He outlines how LLMs excel at coding because of extraordinarily rich public data (28M repositories, 1B+ commits annually), with targeted improvements rapidly making them useful for developers. Math became the next frontier, with models reaching olympiad-level performance primarily through curating huge high-quality datasets, rather than just scaling. Science presents a harder challenge: unlike math's text-based substrate, the actual scientific process (experiment design, failures, measurements) is rarely captured in accessible data, and synthetic data can't easily fill this gap since validation requires physical experiments.
I'd argue that law represents the next frontier beyond science, which may explain why frontier labs don't yet evaluate on legal benchmarks. While science faces data challenges, it retains a crucial advantage: experimental verifiability. Even with slow experiments in the absence of sophisticated simulators, we can still test hypotheses against physical reality. Law may prove even more intractable for LLMs. Validating legal reasoning often requires the expensive, time-consuming process of actual litigation, with no simulators available and outcomes depending on human judgment in ways that resist systematic verification.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool new benchmark from @MiniMax_AI: OctoCodingBench
Current coding agent benchmarks only measure whether tasks are completed, not whether agents follow the specified rules and constraints during the process. Users are frustrated when agents produce working code but violate explicit instructions like naming conventions, safety protocols, or team standards.
MiniMax introduces OctoCodingBench, which evaluates agents on both Check-level Success Rate (individual rule compliance) and Instance-level Success Rate (adherence to all rules simultaneously). This process-oriented approach measures whether agents follow constraints from system prompts, user queries, repository specifications, and project documentation.
Main findings:
- Models follow individual rules well but struggle combining them
- Instruction-following degrades significantly over multiple conversation turns
- Open-source models now rival top closed-source performance levels

Many low resource languages are notoriously left behind by modern AI through lower coverage in training data and less efficient tokenization.

- They used a two-stage fine-tuning process that combines high-quality synthetic data with a reinforcement learning phase optimized by reward models.
- The results are particularly impressive for the open-source community, as the smaller fine-tuned models often match or exceed the performance of much larger baselines, making high-quality translation more accessible.
- The models show consistent gains across 55 language pairs, including significant improvements in low-resource languages like Swahili and Icelandic.
- Interestingly, even without specific multimodal training during these stages, the models retain strong capabilities for translating text within images.

summary:
End of last year @HuggingFace released FinePDFs, an enormous pretraining dataset of 475M PDFs on the web.
They also released a very illustrative blog post explaining much of the background related to PDF processing!
Below are my main takeaways.
- PDFs are especially important for long-context training (one in four PDFs is more than 1MB, the average is ~5.3k chars with the 95th percentile at ~68k)
- Less than 1% of documents in CommonCrawl are PDFs
- So much of the old internet is dead: about 2/3 before 2020
- Extraction speed is extremely important at this scale, so they trained a classifier to discriminate the PDFs that need OCR on a GPU leaving most of the PDFs for cheap CPU extraction
- LMDeploy is a promising inference framework alternative to vLLM if your model is supported
- They applied model-based filtering by labeling 300k samples with Qwen3‑235B‑A22B‑Instruct‑2507 and then distilling the labels to a small bert model (ModernBERT-large)
- The source distribution is extremely long-tail: There is many CDNs, government and legal sources (NRC, govinfo, state legislatures, Justia) and a solid block of science (arXiv, APS, Copernicus, MDPI)
Overall, creating a large-scale high-quality PDF dataset requires an intricate and long pipeline of many steps including many classifiers, extractors and cleaners.
The blog post is well worth a read!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_hV_TBbkAAdNUO.jpg

[1/2] Lost in Translation: Real clients say 'scammed' when they mean illegal fundraising, 'cheated' when they mean breach of contract. Legal AI must decode emotional language into statutory terms.
@Alibaba_Qwen's new benchmark PLawBench finally measures LLMs on this challenge.
In real-world consultations, clients describe situations ambiguously, omit critical details, or conceal unfavorable facts. Effective legal work depends on iterative questioning to clarify intent and reconstruct what actually matters legally.
PLawBench replaces clean case descriptions with messy client-perspective narratives: unreasonable demands, incorrect terminology, and misleading information that mirror authentic lawyer-client interactions.
The results reveal no universal winner. GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5 excel at instruction adherence and procedural stability, while Gemini and Qwen3-Max outperform on deep logical deduction, suggesting a trade-off between safe generation and reasoning depth.
Super cool new work by @AlibabaGroup and their collaborators; easily one of the best legal AI papers I have seen in a while!
This seems to me like the first time a big lab focuses on the legal domain. Maybe we'll soon see Qwen3.5 optimized for law!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
How to win best paper awards?
Find the idea
- have good research taste: know what to work on
- get good collaborators: catch mistakes early (how to get them? spend time into writing cold emails)
- read papers: why? 1. know what is possible, 2. what to do to get some result, 3. build on the paper
- ignore papers: don't be biased by bad ideas, hard to know what to discard and what to keep
- work on the most important problem in your field
- be fast: the exact same paper written 6 months earlier is the difference between groundbreaking and boring
- find your comparative advantage: e.g., I am good at data work but bad a modeling work
- get lucky: 1. you stumbled upon a good idea, 2. be uniquely positioned to solve the problem
Do the research
- get lucky again: the idea actually works
- kill papers that are not working: start on the hardest subproblem to derisk (I find this the hardest!)
- kill low impact papers: finish fast as blog posts or workshop papers
- reprioritize ruthlessly: immediately drop what you're working on and pivot to higher impact project (this is super hard because you have to be confident in your taste)
- put in unreasonable amounts of effort: good papers don't have poorly performed experiments
- have focus: on the core idea, nothing else
- the paper should be in a local optimum: no obvious improvements visible
Write it down
- have focus: on the core idea, nothing else
- know your reader: pick a particular one and write tailored to that reader
- your title is not so important: convince with the science, not clickbait
- your abstract is: convey sense of importance
- write a good intro: your results don't matter if the reader doesn't get the problem
- each figure must stand on its own: because most reader skim through the paper
- write a good conclusion: moment of reflection, not just abstract in past tense
- write well: read it out loud to catch things you would not otherwise
After writing
- get lucky one last time: 1. it's not too early, 2. it's still a hot topic, 3. nobody else did it first, 4. the committee likes it
- be persistent: often multiple submissions are required
Obviously don't just have the award as a goal, just use this to write impactful papers!
Great post by Nicholas Carlini!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Nice blog post by Jack Morris on embedding models!
Main learnings:
- Embedding models have not been scaled up as much as generative models
- Scaling data does not work well naively because inevitably we will get (wrong) gradients on false negatives
- Human labels are super expensive, but we can approximate them with LLMs.
Full procedure:
1. Gather all the text pairs you can find.
2. For each query Q, filter the top-k using BM25 and embeddings. Gain some set of K documents {D_1, ..., D_K}, relevant to Q.
3. Run each pair (D_*, Q) through an LLM to figure out if D is truly a negative example or not.
4. Output: a perfectly-labeled retrieval dataset that's arbitrarily scalable.
5. Train the model using exact softmax and coordinate ascent.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Today we're taking a closer look at earlier synthetic datasets. Which subparts actually drive performance there?
For Nemotron-HQ-Synth (green) we see that the main driver is the Diverse QA Pairs prompt. It is also the only prompt that outperforms the strong DCLM baseline.
For BeyondWeb (red) we see lower variance but continue is slightly better. Both summarize and continue are super simple (< 25 words). The continue prompt just says that the LLM should continue writing the seed document, quite a neat idea.
This is already an early indication that complicated long prompts don't add benefits for synthetic rephrasing.
Tomorrow we're gonna discuss the prompts in more detail.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDtHh1ebwAA2Z25.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Coming closer to the heart of FinePhrase, the prompts.
We tried 9 different prompts rephrasing the seed documents into polished synthetic data. Each prompt provides a different perspective.
Four prompts outperform the DCLM baseline: Math, Table, FAQ and Tutorial.
This experiment really drives the point home about how important the prompts are. The difference between the worst (commentary) and the best (math) is 0.3 points or 25%!
Tomorrow it's all about model sizes.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyR2AlbwAADRDp.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Do we get any benefits by rephrasing with larger models?
The 270m model is clearly worse than the others. But surprisingly, there is not a big difference afterwards. The 1B model seems to be enough.
This is great news, it allows us to rephrase orders of magnitude more data with the same compute budget!
Tomorrow we're investigating which prompts and models are the most chatty.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HD3aP4lbYAAmWKB.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Today we are taking a closer look at the data generated by different models and prompts.
Table leads to fairly short outputs across model families.
Math is also fairly short, but shows more variance with Gemma-3-270m as a notable outlier generating >1k tokens on average.
Tutorial leads to an even spread across output length but still with a bias towards shorter outputs.
FAQ causes the longest documents on average with many models hovering around 700 tokens.
Overall SmolLM2 and Qwen3 tend to be on the shorter side whereas Gemma-3 tends to be more verbose.
Tomorrow we're discussing how to optimize throughput to save $$$ on data generation at scale.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HD8XeEnbAAAbhqi.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Now that we know how to create good synthetic data, how can we generate it in large quantities?
We want to generate as much data as possible given our budget. This means we have to optimize throughput as much as we can.
The default settings for vLLM are not always optimal, so we developed a benchmarking setup that allows us to sweep the most promising parameters.
In total we ran 800+ experiments just to find the best setups! Since each experiments takes less than 2 hours, we get a huge ROI from them.
For example, we were able to find parameters that speed up SmolLM2-1.7B by 75%. This optimization saved us 400+ H100 days on generating the final FinePhrase dataset or more than $25k!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
📰🎓 New extension to the Synthetic Data Playbook!
We trained 60 models to answer one question: does generator size actually matter for synthetic pretraining data? The answer is yes, but only if your student is big enough to notice.
We swept Gemma-3 generators (270M to 27B) across four student sizes (0.5B to 6.2B) and found:
- A 0.5B student squashes all generators into a tiny band (spread: 0.004). It literally can't tell good data from great data.
- At 2.9B, three tiers emerge: 270M is clearly worst, 1B sits in the middle, 4B+ generators form a top group.
- Going past 2.9B to 6.2B doesn't widen the gap much further. 2.9B is the sweet spot.
The big takeaway: if you're evaluating synthetic data with a small proxy model, your conclusions might be wrong. We thought generator size didn't matter past 1B. Turns out our 1.7B student was just too small to see the difference. A 2.9B student reveals quality gaps that the 1.7B student compressed into noise.
Pick your evaluation model carefully. It changes what you can measure.
Full interactive analysis in the updated playbook:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFT50UOaAAArEoD.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Happy to share that our paper "Parity-Aware Byte-Pair Encoding: Improving Cross-lingual Fairness in Tokenization" was accepted to #ACL2026 in San Diego 🇺🇸!
When you use ChatGPT or Claude, you pay per token. But did you know that tokenization is wildly unfair across languages? Standard algorithms like BPE learn by counting what appears most frequently in training data, which overwhelmingly favors English and other high-resource languages. The result: speakers of lower-resource languages see their text split into more tokens, paying higher API costs for the same message.
Vocabulary utilization measures what fraction of a tokenizer's vocabulary actually gets used for each language. When utilization is low, the model has failed to allocate meaningful tokens to that language, fragmenting words into inefficient subwords.
We introduce Parity-Aware BPE, which at every step asks: "Which language is currently getting the worst compression?" It then selects merges that specifically help that language. The result is dramatically fairer vocabulary allocation across high, medium, and low-resource languages compared to Classical BPE.
Best part? Models trained with our tokenizer perform just as well on downstream tasks, while achieving near-perfect parity in tokenization costs. Same performance, fairer access.
Joint work with @negarforoutan, @clara__meister, @DebjitPaul2, @sina_ahm, @ABosselut, and @RicoSennrich.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFZEjBea8AEaG1L.jpg

summary:
Community asked, we delivered. 🚀
We just released almost 7TB of raw rephrased data from #FinePhrase to enable further experimentation and analysis. Code is also public for full transparency and reproducibility.
We're using the new Hugging Face Buckets feature for this release. Unlike git-based repos, buckets provide S3-like object storage with content-addressable deduplication. Perfect for this use case because:
- No version control overhead for massive files (7TB would be painful in git)
- Fast, mutable storage for artifacts that don't need history tracking
- Simple CLI and Python API for syncing, filtering, and browsing
- Server-side file copying without re-uploading
@ratishsp ran a detailed quality analysis on the dataset and found some interesting patterns. Format compliance on tables was rough, hallucination rates were high across splits. Makes sense since the rephrasing was done by a 1.7B model.
Weird thing: models pretrained on this data still hit decent benchmark scores after 20B and 100B tokens, even with the quality issues. We covered some of this in the original blog post, but there's clearly more to understand here.
That's exactly why we're releasing everything. If you want to dig into:
- How synthetic data quality actually impacts pretraining
- Why benchmark performance doesn't always track with perceived quality
- Better filtering or multi-round rephrasing approaches
- The counterintuitive relationship between data quality and model performance
Now you can.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
The Synthetic Data Playbook is now a paper! 📄
We trained >100 models across different rephrasing strategies, generator sizes, and source data to figure out what actually matters for synthetic pretraining.
Key findings:
- Prompt design drives performance more than anything else
- Structured pedagogical formats beat simple paraphrasing
- Generator size beyond 1B gives negligible gains for most prompts
- Source quality matters less than you'd think when you have solid mix-in data
- Generative diversity beats formatting consistency
- Original web data is still essential for commonsense reasoning and linguistic variety
The result: FinePhrase, a 486B-token dataset that cuts costs 30× while outperforming established baselines.
We open sourced everything for full reproducibility. Dataset, ablation data, generation framework, code, benchmark results, all training hyperparameters, and prompt templates.
Shoutout to @_gucciiiii for leading this effort!

He just open-sourced a 590GB dataset containing 8 million SEC EDGAR filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, etc.) and 43 billion tokens from 20 years of publicly traded company financial data. Includes both raw and parsed plaintext versions plus metadata.
Unofficial API providers charge hundreds of dollars per month for this data with strict rate limits. The official SEC EDGAR system limits you to 10 requests/second, meaning crawling 8 million filings takes over 10 days. This dataset gives you everything pre-crawled, cleaned, and parsed for free on Hugging Face.
You can train financial LLMs on 43B tokens of real corporate filings without paying API fees, build retrieval systems that understand SEC filing structure and terminology, fine-tune models on specific filing types (10-K annual reports, 8-K material events, etc.), or create benchmarks for financial document understanding and reasoning. Gives researchers and developers free access to domain data that's been locked behind paywalls, keeping financial AI development open when everything else is closing up.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Heading to #ICLR2026 in Rio 🇧🇷
Looking forward to meeting old and new friends. Reach out if you want to chat!
We're presenting LEXam, a new benchmark for long-form legal reasoning. Come see us in Poster Session 1 in Pavilion 3 on Thursday, Apr 23, at 10:30!
Can't make it to the conference? Here's more details about LEXam:
Long-form legal reasoning is still a serious problem for LLMs, even with all the recent progress on test-time scaling. So we built a benchmark that actually measures it.
LEXam comes from 340 real law exams across 116 courses, covering different subjects and degree levels. 7,537 questions total in English and German. Mix of open-ended long-form questions and multiple-choice.
What makes it different: the open questions include explicit guidance on what legal reasoning approach is expected. Issue spotting, rule recall, rule application. Not just "answer this question" but "show your work the way a law student would."
Key findings:
- Current LLMs struggle hard with open questions that need structured, multi-step legal reasoning
- The dataset differentiates clearly between models with different capability levels
- LLM-as-a-Judge with human expert validation can evaluate reasoning steps accurately and consistently
- This gives us a scalable way to measure legal reasoning quality beyond simple accuracy
The evaluation setup is the interesting part. We deployed an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm with rigorous human validation. Turns out model-generated reasoning steps can be assessed in a way that aligns closely with how human experts would judge them.
That matters because legal reasoning isn't about getting the right answer, it's about following the right process to get there.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Switzerland just voted to abolish the marriage penalty (54% yes) and rejected universal civic service (84% no). Both votes are deeply gendered, so I tried something: I asked an AI to research gender equality in Switzerland from scratch, every dimension it could find.
Gender equality isn't a single scoreboard. It's asymmetric.
Women in Switzerland earn 8.4% less (median), receive 31% lower pensions, do 10 more hours of unpaid care per week, and face 70% of domestic violence.
Men have a suicide rate 2.6x higher, make up 83% of the homeless, are graded lower for the same school work, and still owe mandatory military service while the civic duty initiative just failed at 84% no.
Both of these are true at the same time.
GPT-5.5 gave up after 3 subreports. I told it three times to keep going. It never obeyed.
Then I gave the same task to Claude Opus 4.7. It spawned subagents, chased down 365 sources, and produced 80 subreports on topics from wage gap decomposition to male suicide, from femicide statistics to boys' school performance, from the motherhood penalty to custody outcomes, from women in tech to men's DV shelters.
Opus deserves the top spot on the METR benchmark, it's just independent for much longer!

The full synthesis:

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
"Please stop hiring agents as interns!", HR just slacked me.
Too late. We just hired a physics intern at @HuggingFace!
physics-intern just set a new SOTA on CritPt, the hardest physics benchmark for LLMs:
→ Gemini 3.1 Pro: 17.7% → 31.4% (new #1 on the leaderboard, beating GPT 5.5 Pro)
→ Kimi K2.6 (open weights): 8.0% → 21.4% (best open-weights result, beating DeepSeek V4 Pro Max at 12.9%)
CritPt contains 70 research-level theoretical physics problems spanning quantum field theory, general relativity, and statistical mechanics. No compiler, no test suite, no proof checker. Just long chains of reasoning where a single wrong sign kills the whole derivation. Frontier models at max reasoning barely crack 30%.
How does it work?
9 specialized agents simulate the full scientific process: surveying literature, planning a research strategy, running derivations, writing verification code, and adversarially reviewing every result at every stage. Just like a real research lab, fully automated, minus the toxic advisors.
First we hired an ml-intern. Now we hired a physics intern. HR is not pleased.
Learn more:

summary:
Interesting new (to me) take on the "AI automates your job" debate by Alex Imas
I keep discussing this topic with coworkers and friends, on different ends of the doomer spectrum. Refreshing to read a more calming take here :)
TLDR:
- AI won't end scarcity, it shifts what's scarce
- Richer people want status, exclusivity, and human connection
- Structural change shifts workers between sectors, not out
- Rising income redirects spending toward high-income-elasticity goods
- AI involvement undermines perceived uniqueness and exclusivity
- "Relational sector" grows: value tied to the human provider
- Future durable jobs are relational, not commodity production

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
We are releasing Carbon: a crazy fast DNA model
Carbon is 275x faster than the next best model. So fast you can process the whole human genome on a single GPU in <2 days.
Here are the tricks we used:
When modelling DNA sequences a lot of the performance comes down to tokenizing the sequences in a smart way. BPE tokenizer struggle because there are no whitespaces and character (called base in DNA) level tokenizers waste a lot of compute on too many tokens.
Carbon is built with a unique tokenizer: we split sequences in chunks of 6 bases, but during both training and inference we can work with single base resolution. That's similar to having word tokens but resolving them at the character level. All possible thanks to the DNA tokens unique structure.
The architecture combined with the tokenizer makes the model 275x faster than the previous SoTA (Evo2) at this size.
We built an interactive demo so you can explore how the model can generate DNA sequences, investigate the structure of genes, predict the effect of mutations, generate and fold proteins and even reconstruct parts of the tree of life.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2056768792491933696/img/bLgCFA_PvlE7yOlb.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2056768792491933696/vid/avc1/398x270/UfnCNPI3Fy7dQMza.mp4?tag=27
