title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Introducing Carbon 🧬 a family of open generative DNA foundation models. Carbon-3B matches Evo2-7B while running 250x faster at inference. It can generate new DNA sequences and score the functional impact of mutations, zero-shot.
We borrowed a lot from how modern LLMs are trained, but DNA isn't language. Genomes are noisy, redundant, and shaped by evolution rather than communication. So we adjusted the recipe:
Tokenizer. Most genomic models tokenize at the nucleotide/character level, which blows up sequence length. BPE is the obvious LLM-style fix, but it doesn't behave well on DNA. We use deterministic 6-mer tokens (one token = 6 nucleotides): 6× shorter sequences and cheaper attention.
Training loss. With 6-mer tokens, cross-entropy scores a prediction that gets 5/6 nucleotides right the same as one that's completely wrong. This gets brittle late in training and produces loss spikes. We switch mid-training to a more flexible factorized loss (FNS).
Data. Genomes are mostly sparse, repetitive background. We curate down to a staged functional DNA + mRNA mixture, with every ratio chosen by ablation, like mixing a web corpus, but for biology.
We're releasing the models, training data, training code, evaluation suite, and a demo to play with.
More details in the technical report:
Demo to play with the model, with a biology primer for our ML friends ;)
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2056766427558731776/img/my4n_MYmJYISq-zs.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2056766427558731776/vid/avc1/398x270/ENfBNgeqfLJQeSZi.mp4?tag=27

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Excited to share Carbon, the most efficient foundation models for generative DNA 🧬. Carbon-3B matches the performance of leading DNA models, while being over 275x faster at inference!
We trained Carbon on 1T tokens of high-quality DNA sequences and folded in all the tricks of modern LLMs:
- RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE
- long-context expansion
- GQA
However, training DNA models is cursed compared to LLMs: most of the public data is noisy, BPE doesn't work, cross-entropy loss blows up after a few hundred billion tokens, and there's basically no public evals for such models :(
We solved all these issues over the past few months and you can read all about them in our interactive explainer:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIsk-uhXoAEpuP0.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
LEXTREME, the first multilingual legal NLP benchmark, just grew to 12 datasets!
Now it also covers the Ukrainian language with Judgment Prediction for Ukrainian Court Decisions. The full dataset is huge, containing ~100M cases across three periods: Pre-war, Hybrid war and Full-scale.
Pre-war (2008–2013): All 832 courts operational across all 25 oblasts + Crimea. Criminal docket dominated by property crimes (theft, fraud), drug offenses. Administrative courts handle tax disputes, pension cases. Outcome distribution relatively stable year-to-year.
Hybrid war (2014–2021): In 2014, Ukraine lost ~40 courts in Crimea and parts of Donetsk/Luhansk, so they disappear from the registry. New case categories emerge: internally displaced persons' property rights, ATO veteran benefits, anti-terrorist operation proceedings. Criminal code amended with new articles on terrorism (258), separatism (110). The case-type mix shifts measurably, but the fundamental court procedure stays the same.
Full-scale (2022–2026): Martial law declared, changing procedural timelines, appeal rules, and judge availability. Military criminal cases explode: AWOL (art. 407 KK), desertion (art. 408), draft evasion (art. 336), insubordination (art. 402). New Criminal Code articles added: collaborationism (111-1), aiding the aggressor state (111-2). Administrative offense courts now handle mass mobilization-related cases (art. 210-1 KUpAP). Several more courts in newly occupied territories go offline. The guilty and plea_deal labels see a significant frequency increase compared to earlier epochs.
Thanks for this contribution by Volodymyr Ovcharov!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIxX-aibgAE8FQ8.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
🇨🇭 New in @HuggingFace LightEval: Swiss legal tasks are now supported natively!
You can now evaluate LLMs on Swiss legal translation and summarization out of the box, covering SLDS and all three SwiLTra-Bench task types.
The tasks:
📜 Law translations (slt): translating Swiss federal legislation across de, fr, it, rm, and en, at law, article, and paragraph level.
⚖️ Headnote translations (sdst): translating Federal Supreme Court decision summaries across de, fr, it, at decision, regeste, and text level.
📰 Press release translations (sscprt): translating Federal Supreme Court press releases across de, fr, it.
📝 Headnote generation (slds): generating concise German, French, or Italian headnotes from full Swiss landmark decisions. From SLDS, a dataset of 20K Federal Supreme Court rulings with headnotes in all three languages.
Evaluation goes beyond lexical overlap (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) with dedicated LLM-as-a-Judge metrics (SwiLTra-Judge) that align well with human expert assessments.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Legal work is the next frontier for AI progress.
The best models on @Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark are shown below. Unlike coding and math where you can verify outputs automatically, legal work doesn't have that advantage. That's why we're seeing much lower success rates here.
They did an interesting analysis around the behavior of the different agents. GPT 5.5 for example spends much more time reading than Opus 4.7. Even across different generations of the same model there is quite a bit of variance (e.g., Opus 4.6 vs 4.7 or GPT 5.4 vs 5.5), telling us that different post-training makes a big difference.
They also analyze what specific sequences lead to improvements or degradations in performance. For example, targeted retrieval leads to 0.3 points increase whereas drafting without review leads to 1.2 points drop in all-pass score.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Excited to speak about SwiLTra-Bench at the @maxplancklaw Artificial Justice Series next week!
In Switzerland legal translation is uniquely important due to the country’s four official languages and requirements for multilingual legal documentation.
However, this process traditionally relies on professionals who must be both legal experts and skilled translators—creating bottlenecks and impacting effective access to justice.
To address this challenge, we introduce SwiLTra-Bench, a comprehensive multilingual benchmark of over 180K aligned Swiss legal translation pairs comprising laws, headnotes, and press releases across all Swiss languages along with English, designed to evaluate LLM-based translation systems.
Our systematic evaluation reveals that frontier models achieve superior translation performance across all document types, while specialized translation systems excel specifically in laws but under-perform in headnotes.
Through rigorous testing and human expert validation, we demonstrate that while fine-tuning open SLMs significantly improves their translation quality, they still lag behind the best zero-shot prompted frontier models such as Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
Additionally, we present SwiLTra-Judge, a specialized LLM evaluation system that aligns best with human expert assessments.
Thanks for the invitation Oskar von Cossel!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Synthetic Data Playbook update!
TLDR: Most diversity scores don't predict synthetic-data quality. G-Vendi is the exception.
I added four diversity metrics across 83 synthetic-pretraining experiments: Vendi Score, mean intra-set cosine similarity, and near-duplicate rate (all on bge-base-en-v1.5 sentence embeddings), plus G-Vendi from the Prismatic Synthesis paper. The selling point if any of them works: rank a candidate rephrasing recipe from 1000 generated samples, instead of generating millions of tokens and training a student model end-to-end.
The three semantic metrics fall apart on aggregate downstream performance. Vendi correlates negatively (ρ = −0.21), mean cosine similarity positively (ρ = +0.23, but that's just −Vendi by construction), near-duplicate rate essentially zero. None of them is a usable overall predictor.
G-Vendi flips the script. Instead of asking "do these samples look different?", it asks "would training on each of them push the model's weights in different directions?". You backprop the cross-entropy loss through a frozen proxy LLM (I used Qwen3-0.6B), sketch the resulting gradient, L2-normalise and then take the Vendi Score in that feature space. Across the same 83 experiments, G-Vendi correlates positively with the macro score (ρ = +0.26) and is the single best predictor for reasoning of any metric I tested (ρ = +0.38), beating every quality classifier and semantic-diversity variant.
But none of this displaces DCLM-difference. Even G-Vendi explains only ~7% of variance on the macro score, while DCLM-difference (output minus input quality score) still wins overall (ρ = +0.61). Diversity metrics complement quality classifiers, they don't replace them. The shortcut around training-and-evaluating still doesn't exist.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJkn4BoaUAEj4yP.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
In our #finephrase audit across six math rephrasers, the cleanest one made the worst pretraining data.
We just extended our finephrase blog with a quantitative format-adherence audit on the math-rephrasing experiments. We compared six small instruction-tuned models as math-problem rephrasers on FineWeb-Edu: SmolLM2 (1.7B), Qwen3 (1.7B), Llama 3.2 (1B), Gemma 3 (1B), Falcon 3 (1B), and Granite 3 (1B). 10,000 outputs per model, every N op N = N arithmetic statement extracted and verified, plus five cheap heuristics for problem shape and source grounding.
By every measure of surface polish, Qwen3 dominates:
• 99.7% of outputs have a Problem/Solution structure
• 98.9% use numbered or bulleted step-by-step formatting
• 78.9% per-equation arithmetic accuracy
• 30.2% contain a fully verifiable correct equation
SmolLM2 looks chaotic by comparison:
• Only 32% have Problem/Solution structure
• 23% contain ZERO digits (genuine off-topic essays about dog sunburn, cooking, history, ...)
• Output length ranges from 1 to 3,540 tokens
• Only 8.1% contain a verifiable equation
And yet, pretraining on SmolLM2's outputs beats pretraining on Qwen3's outputs on downstream benchmarks.
Why?
Template collapse. Across 10,000 outputs, Qwen3 has only 40 distinct first-10-character openings (most being a variant of "**Problem:"). SmolLM2 has 1,897. The chart below tracks "outputs sharing the most common prefix" across prefix lengths 2 to 60. Qwen3 stays glued to a plateau of about 7,600 out of 10,000 well past the 10-character mark.
The full audit table shows the structural-vs-content gap across all metrics. Surface polish doesn't even translate to math correctness: every model gets 20 to 40 percent of its own equations wrong. And the model whose outputs stay closest to the source documents (topic Jaccard 0.187, more than 2x Qwen3's 0.093) is Gemma 3. Qwen3's rigid template often invents fictional scenarios that drift from the input.
Takeaway: for pretraining data, diversity beats consistency. A messier rephraser that produces varied, source-grounded text can outperform a polished one that produces formulaic, fictional math. What pretraining picks up isn't the correctness of any individual word problem; it's the format and topic variety in the rephrased corpus, consistent with the WRAP finding that paraphrase diversity drives downstream gains.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-mQzMb0AEYSkj.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-mQ-PbwAA-aJt.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
New FinePhrase result: the best synthetic-to-real ratio for pretraining isn't 50/50.
Quick context: FinePhrase is our open 486B-token synthetic pretraining dataset. We take FineWeb-Edu web text, rephrase it with a small 1.7B model (SmolLM2) into four structured formats (FAQs, math problems, tables, tutorials), and then train on a mix of original and synthetic data. The whole recipe came out of 90 controlled pretraining experiments.
The new question we tackled: how much of that mix should actually be synthetic? We swept the synthetic fraction from 10% to 90% for each format. Every format's optimum sits higher than the uniform 50/50, and it's format-dependent: tables peak at 70% synthetic, math at 80%, FAQ and tutorials at 60%. The curves climb to their peak and then plateau rather than collapsing, so there's a wide safe band and no sign of the "too much synthetic = model collapse" failure mode.
This also sets a new state of the art among synthetic pretraining data. Our best config (tables at 70% synthetic) is 31% better and reaches the same quality 3.2x faster than REWIRE, the strongest rephrasing baseline, which used a 70B-parameter model. We get there with a 1.7B rephraser that also generates tokens roughly 30x cheaper.
A caveat: these results are at small scale (1.7B parameters, 21B training tokens) so might not transfer to larger training runs.
Read the updated playbook:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKIrASMbYAAQzdg.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKIrAdwaAAAfknj.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Does the model rewriting your web text quietly copy benchmark questions into your training set? We audited 56 corpora to find out.
Synthetic pretraining data has an obvious failure mode: the rephraser potentially regurgitates memorized benchmark questions and quietly contaminates your eval.
So we ran a 10-gram contamination audit across our rephrased corpora (8 prompts x 6 small rephrasers) plus the source and baseline datasets, against our 12 benchmarks.
The fair comparison is flagged documents per billion tokens, since we sampled every corpus to the same 5B-token budget. On that measure:
→ 5 of our 6 rephrasers leak LESS than the FineWeb-Edu-HQ data they rewrite (841/Btok). Only Llama 3.2 edges above it (864), and the spread across models is tiny.
→ The single most contaminated corpus is the external REWIRE baseline, not any of our rephrased data.
→ And it's all negligible: even REWIRE works out to roughly one flagged document per 500k tokens.
Verdict: no benchmark leakage from rephrasing. The scores are clean.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKTMoLebAAAkVa6.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
New update to the Synthetic Data Playbook: how much of our results is just luck?
Quick refresher: the Synthetic Data Playbook is our open guide to turning noisy web text into state-of-the-art pretraining data, by finding the right prompts, rephrasing models, and infrastructure.
The whole playbook rests on comparing training runs. Recipe A scores a bit higher than recipe B, so A wins. But every score comes from a single run, and training is random (the weight initialization and the order the data arrives both involve a dice roll). So a fair question to ask before trusting any of it: how much does the score move if we change nothing but the random seeds?
We added a dedicated check to find out. We took our headline recipe (FineWeb-Edu-HQ blended 50/50 with table-formatted synthetic data) and the raw baseline it beats, and retrained each one nine times, sweeping the init seed and the data-order seed in a 3×3 grid. Then we repeated the whole thing at four model sizes from 0.5B to 6.2B. 72 from-scratch runs, just to measure noise.
What we found:
- The noise floor is tiny. Scores reproduce to about ±0.002 (roughly 1% wobble) at every model size. The bar doesn't grow as models get bigger.
- The synthetic-data win is not luck. The gain over the raw baseline is 14 to 26 times larger than that noise. There is simply no seed you could pick that erases it.
- Which dice matter? The model's initialization matters more than the order it sees the data. Data ordering is consistently the smallest source of variance.
Synthetic data even stabilizes training. The mixed recipe was more reproducible than the raw-web baseline at every scale.
- This lines up with what the broader community has found training models from scratch across seeds (MultiBERTs, PolyPythias, DataDecide), and it's exactly why we evaluate in cloze format, which is known to cut this kind of measurement noise for small models.
Two things this number doesn't cover. That ±0.002 bar is an aggregate number. Individual benchmarks are far noisier (a 1-point move on DROP is just noise, while the same move on HellaSwag is real), and we only ran the full seed grid on one synthetic recipe, so we treat it as a rule of thumb rather than a guarantee.
The takeaway: the gaps we report in the playbook are real signal, not seed roulette. New interactive chart in the post lets you flip between the scores, the per-seed training curves, and a breakdown of where the variance comes from.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdgs4QbsAALUOs.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdgtCsbEAAHsym.jpg

summary:
Macrodata Labs is launching today to build infrastructure for the robotics data loop.
Robotics is starting to scale. Progress in LLMs and VLMs is making robots more capable, but the data layer behind robotics is still underbuilt.
Physical-world data is messy and fragmented. Every robot, sensor setup, and lab has its own assumptions, and teams still spend too much time writing brittle scripts just to make their data usable.
The hard part is not only collecting more demonstrations. It is turning those demonstrations into datasets teams can train on, inspect, improve, and reuse as their policies and data collection setups change.
We built Refiner as our first step toward better infrastructure for robotics data. It is an open-source framework for turning messy robotics data into scalable, inspectable, training-ready datasets.
Refiner helps teams process demonstrations, add annotations, run reward model scoring, and scale robotics data pipelines from local execution to managed cloud compute on the Macrodata Labs platform.
Starting today, you can use Refiner and the Macrodata Labs platform to make the most out of your robotics data.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
We're launching Macrodata Labs.
Me and @gui_penedo have spent the past three years in the trenches working on data for training LLMs. This gave us a unique perspective on how the field has progressed - from GPT-3-era models capable of little more than simple completions to today, where agents are writing a substantial share of the code being shipped.
This progress was enabled by just two components: scaling data and compute while being extremely deliberate about what data to use and what not to use. Look at failed training runs and ask researchers what caused them - poor data quality is almost always at the top of the list.
While LLMs have undergone this Cambrian explosion, robotics today feels exactly like LLMs did back then. There is still no clear recipe for what will work. Every team has its own opinions on embodiment and architecture, yet they all agree on one thing: the most important problem to solve is data and how to scale it.
Nobody knows yet whether the answer lies in simulation data, egocentric data, IMU data, or something completely different.
Whatever the answer turns out to be, every team still has to go through the same process: acquiring the data, filtering problematic episodes, synchronizing sensor values, annotating episodes using VLMs, splitting episodes into subtasks, or, in the case of egocentric data, extracting 21-DOF hand annotations. Finally, all of this has to be converted into training-ready datasets before training starts as choosing a bad format for training will waste GPU cycles.
These pipelines need to run continuously. Every day, new episodes arrive from in-house data collection efforts and external vendors. Teams not only have to deal with the peculiarities of working with video data, ensuring sensor streams are error-free and avoiding unnecessary video decoding, but also need to support ingestion from whatever formats their data vendors provide.
Many teams are solving these problems today, yet you'll quickly discover that 99% of the solutions are collections of one-off scripts, which everyone hates the moment something goes wrong. Researchers end up digging through repositories trying to find the script that performed a particular operation three months ago, not even knowing whether they're looking at the version that was actually run.
What people want is something as scalable as Spark and as trackable as Weights & Biases.
That is what we created Macrodata Labs to build.
Our first step is Refiner, an open-source framework for processing robotics datasets.
We designed Refiner to help robotics teams turn raw demonstrations into training-ready datasets. Instead of maintaining collections of one-off scripts, teams can use Refiner to ingest heterogeneous robotics data, synchronize sensors, run annotation workflows, extract signals like hand tracking, split trajectories into subtasks, and continuously process new data as it arrives.
Alongside Refiner, we're also launching Refiner Cloud. With a one-line code change, the same pipeline can scale on our platform, with sharding, checkpointing, failure recovery, lineage tracking, and observability built in—so teams can focus on what matters most: data, not infrastructure plumbing.
We're incredibly fortunate to have the support of @airstreet , @DrysdaleVC , OPRTRS Club, @kimaventures , YG (Alex Yazdi), >commit, @Thom_Wolf , and an amazing group of angels from leading AI labs and technology companies who share our belief that data will be one of the defining challenges in robotics.
If this resonates with you, give Refiner a try, and don't hesitate to shoot me a message. We'd love to chat.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKhMRjzWEAExr1M.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Today we’re announcing Macrodata Labs.
Over the last few years, @HKydlicek and I have been turning a large part of the internet into some of the largest open LLM pre-training datasets. Through FineWeb, FineWeb2, FinePDFs, FineTranslations, and related work, we got a front-row seat to how scaling compute and data drove progress in LLMs.
We are starting to see a similar takeoff in robotics.
Building on advances in LLMs and VLMs, robotics is finally starting to scale. But physical data is messy in ways text isn’t: large video files, multi-rate sensors, many different formats, and open questions around what signals to record, which annotations matter, and how to turn all that context into better policies.
That makes data work in robotics especially important. Teams need to extract as much signal as possible from every demonstration, trajectory, video frame, and sensor stream, without rebuilding their whole data stack every time they change robot, sensors, format, or labeling method.
We think the right tooling for this is still missing. That is what we created Macrodata Labs to build. Our first step is Refiner, an open-source framework for processing robotics datasets.
We designed Refiner to handle a variety of robotics formats and help teams extract more signal from each demonstration. It is shipping today with support for hand-tracking, subtask annotation, and reward model scoring.
We are also launching a cloud version of Refiner, so teams can focus on their data instead of infrastructure. With a one-line code change, the same pipeline can scale on our platform, with sharding, checkpointing, model deployments, failure recovery, and detailed observability built in.
We’re fortunate to be backed by Air Street Capital, Drysdale Ventures, OPRTRS club, Kima Ventures, YG (Alex Yazdi), >commit, Thomas Wolf, and many incredible angels from top AI labs and technology companies.
I’m excited to keep exploring how better data work can push the frontier of AI, now in the physical world.
If @macrodata_labs sounds interesting to you, or if you are building in the space, I would love to hear from you.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool new benchmark by Li Zhang et al.: DLawBench!
Most legal benchmarks start from a cleaned and complete case description.
DLawBench starts from the consultation itself.
The client may be emotional, incomplete, uncertain, or hold a biased understanding of the law.
A reliable lawyer model therefore needs to ask follow-up questions, test assumptions, and decide which facts matter before writing legal analysis.
In DLawBench, the model acts as a lawyer. It must interview a client, identify missing or disputed facts, separate the client's beliefs from legally relevant facts, and finally produce a legal memo grounded in what was learned during the dialogue.
Would be great to see the data published on @HuggingFace too 🤗

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
New blog post on harness optimization. We hit Sonnet 4.6 performance with a 7x cost improvement.
Fable 5 was the first frontier model release that evaluated on legal tasks. It only scored 13%, the worst performance among all benchmarks evaluated.
@Harvey released this benchmark called Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) just a month prior. It contains a set of realistic legal matters. Each task gives the agent a closed workspace of documents (contracts, emails, spreadsheets, slide decks) and asks for a concrete deliverable: a diligence memo, an issue list, a redline, a draft. An LLM judge grades the deliverable against a long rubric containing 61 distinct binary criteria each on average.
Many frontier models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro don't surpass 0% all-pass rate (all rubric criteria passed). With automatic harness optimization, we manage to push DeepSeek V4 Pro from 0% to 5% all-pass rate, achieving parity with Sonnet 4.6 for 1/7 of the price.

Many frontier models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro don't surpass 0% all-pass rate (all rubric criteria passed). With automatic harness optimization, we manage to push DeepSeek V4 Pro from 0% to 5% all-pass rate, achieving parity with Sonnet 4.6 for 1/7 of the price.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Don't train the model, evolve the harness.
I read a brilliant blog post from Hugging Face where they took a frozen open model scoring 0% on a hard legal agent benchmark, left its weights alone, and let an automated loop rewrite only the code around it.
That code layer is the harness, the runtime wrapper that feeds the model context, runs its tool calls, and decides when a run ends.
By the time the loop finished, the system had essentially matched Sonnet 4.6 on the benchmark's headline metric, at roughly 7x lower cost per task. Zero weights changed.
The gain existed because of where the model was failing. The judge only grades files saved in the right place under the exact requested filename, and the model kept doing the legal analysis correctly, then saving it under the wrong name, dropping it in a scratch folder, or never writing it at all.
So the 0% was never measuring legal reasoning. It was measuring the harness.
Hand-tuning that layer is slow and model-specific, so they automated it. A Claude proposer adds exactly one mechanism per iteration, and an outer loop keeps it only if it clearly beats the current best, so accepted mechanisms compound.
What the loop discovered says a lot about where agents actually fail.
→ The biggest single gain was file handling, not intelligence. An automatic step that lands the deliverable exactly where the judge expects it beat every prompt change, with zero extra model tokens.
→ Code fixes transferred across models, prompt playbooks did not. The same harness lifted a smaller model from the same family by 14 points, but the tuned prompts hurt a different model family on tasks it could already finish.
→ The harness mattered more than anything else. Same model, same judge, same tasks, and five different harnesses scored anywhere between 3.5% and 80.1%.
The gains do eventually flatten, and the remaining misses look like real capability gaps. At some point the wrapper runs out of tricks and the model has to carry the work.
But the lesson holds. A benchmark score measures the model and its harness together, and until the harness is fixed, it's impossible to know which one failed.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] We just got an award at #ACL2026 for our Parity-Aware BPE paper!
When AI systems process text, they first break it into chunks called tokens. The standard method for deciding how to chunk text (called BPE) learns from frequency: chunks that appear often in the training data get treated efficiently.
Since training data is dominated by languages like English, those languages get compact, sensible tokenizations, while lower-resource languages end up chopped into many more tokens, often in ways that ignore how the language actually works.
This matters practically: more tokens means more computation and higher costs, so speakers of underrepresented languages literally pay more to use the same AI systems.
We propose a fix called Parity-aware BPE. Instead of always picking the chunk that helps compression overall (which mostly benefits dominant languages), our version repeatedly asks: which language is currently getting the worst deal?
Then it picks the chunk that most helps *that* language. It sacrifices a tiny bit of overall efficiency in exchange for fairness across languages.
The results: inequality between languages (measured with the Gini coefficient, the same statistic used for income inequality) drops by up to 89%, while overall compression barely suffers and the AI models trained with it perform just as well.
Great to have been part of an amazing author team: @negarforoutan, @clara__meister, @DebjitPaul2, @sina_ahm, @ABosselut,
@RicoSennrich

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Super influential and well written at the same time as usual!
Quoting @a1zhang
Transformers struggle to generalize to tasks they were not explicitly trained on. Instead, we propose in 2026 that it is the job of the harness to generalize through composition.
We observe a powerful property when training RLMs: for tasks with shared structure that look different, the root model naturally learns the same trajectory, meaning it views the two task trajectories as the same! In other words, the Transformer does not need additional generalization capabilities to transfer capabilities from one task to the other, the harness induces it.
We find that well-designed harnesses form a quotient set over task trajectories, meaning their individual LLM calls can see structurally “similar” tasks as near-identical, token-for-token! Harnesses can effectively generalize for the Transformer during training, without relying on any intrinsic generalization capability from the model.
For example, RLMs can see problems of different lengths as the same: we show that RLMs can train exclusively on short tasks, and fully generalize to similar but unseen tasks 8-32x longer because it produces near identical trajectories for both.
Taking this further, we show that tasks across different domains (e.g. math solutions vs. essay writing) that share a decomposition strategy exhibit the same generalization effect. RLMs can train on the problem of finding which essays belong to the same author and improve performance on finding math problems that share similar solutions.
The full blogpost, experiments, and discussion are in the thread below.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Codex is overoptimised for large models: it ranks 2nd out of 10 for GLM 5.2 but drops to 9th place for Gemma-4!
Almost all the effort in this field goes into tuning the weights. We wanted to know how much of the final number is decided by the harness wrapped around them instead, so we ran 10 coding agent harnesses against two models on SWE-bench Pro.
A lot, it turns out. Swapping the harness moves pass@1 from 23% to 52% on GLM-5.2, and from 15% to 36% on Gemma 4 26B-A4B: a wider gap than most model releases buy you.
And the ranking does not transfer. The rank correlation between the two models' harness leaderboards is -0.05, which is to say: none.
Codex is not alone in this. Every harness shipped by a model vendor drops on the small model — Codex 2nd to 9th, Claude Code 3rd to 7th, Qwen Code 4th to 6th — while the model-agnostic ones climb: crush 7th to 1st, opencode 8th to 2nd, pi 9th to 4th.
The clearest case is crush, 7th on GLM-5.2 and 1st on Gemma 4. Run the identical scaffold on both and the small model wins by 4 points at a twelfth of the price, $0.30 per task against $3.61.
Gemma 4's best harness beats GLM-5.2's four worst. A 26B model in the right scaffold is not far off a 744B model in the wrong one.
Cost per solved task: $0.84 for Gemma 4 + crush at 36%. The cheapest GLM-5.2 setup that scores as well is openclaw at 38%, for $7.05.
Output tokens per task span 16k to 621k across harnesses: a 39x spread in what you pay for, buying a 2x spread in what you get.
97% of input tokens are re-sent conversation prefix, so prompt caching is super important.
The setup: every harness run against both models on the same 250 SWE-bench Pro tasks, one rollout each, priced at list API rates for the tokens each one actually spent. In the plot, a dark ring means the pairing sits on the Pareto frontier across both models and a faded dot means you could score higher for less elsewhere; 2 of the 10 harnesses (goose and hermes) are left out of the figure for legibility

More cool work on automated research replication!
They introduce Replica, a 310-task benchmark where agents must recreate redacted results figures from 100 ML and AI-for-science papers under a 60-minute, limited-GPU budget; a task-specific LLM rubric judges both the plot and the scientific quality of the underlying experiment.
The authors post-train a 27B model, Faraday, with GRPO to orchestrate a coding agent, reporting higher average replication scores than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5/Codex: 0.856 vs. 0.828/0.796 on ML tasks and 0.791 vs. 0.748/0.729 on held-out AI-for-science tasks.
The core claim is that training on underspecified replication work teaches an agent more rigorous, transferable scientific behavior such as implementing the actual mechanism rather than faking expected outputs.
I found it quite interesting that a small model (Faraday) can direct a much larger one (GPT 5.5).
They also found that recent papers are harder to replicate possibly due to recent papers needing more compute.
Read the paper:
Quoting @joelniklaus
Stop what you're doing and read this blog post now, this is such a cool project!
TLDR: @HuggingFace and @askalphaxiv ran a hackathon where 1,200 people pointed coding agents at a third of ICML 2026 and tried to reproduce every paper claim by claim. About half of the examined papers had something verified, a quarter had something falsified or contested, and a handful of the falsifications are serious, including a spotlight paper whose central bound is simply wrong. The reproductions themselves were sometimes wrong too, and sorting that out still took humans.
I think we should have automated agent based reproductions as a default first step in the conference reviewing process!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
I really think we need a centralized organisation that acts as a source of truth for benchmarking!
And with the recent surge in importance of harnesses this gets even more important imo.
Let me explain why.
Already back when we just evaluated LLMs we had a reproducibility crisis.
System prompt, quantization, temperature, top_p, reasoning effort (not even standardized across providers), and other variables can all drastically change performance.
There are so many sources of variance that most runs are not comparable even when targeting the same benchmark!
So we need really standardization to compare models confidently.
Adding harnesses into the mix makes this even more unwieldy. Suddenly we add a whole new source of variance, not even speaking of the infrastructure where we run tasks, differently defined tools, etc.
I only see two options:
1) We need to converge on very clear evaluation standards as a field including an open evaluation harness and reproducible reasoning effort, or
2) we need one central organisation emerging that provides the necessary infrastructure to compare models across benchmarks and harnesses
Quoting @joelniklaus
We need @ArtificialAnlys for harnesses!
Cool to see this kind of interest in harness evaluation, makes it clear to me that this is still an underexplored area.
We have lots of evaluations that compare LLMs but this gets less and less meaningful just by itself because the harness it operates in makes such a huge difference. We need to know what harness LLMs are evaluated in and standardize it if we want to really get the full picture of how good an LLM performs for a task.
Ideally, we go a step further and select a few top harnesses and evaluate each model inside all of them and measure the spread similar to the recent Qwen 3.8 release.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
For Muse-Glimmer-30B, harness choice is a no-brainer: OpenCode sits at the high-performance, low-cost edge.
To test this, I evaluated 10 agent harnesses on the same 50 held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks for three trials each, producing 1,500 scored attempts.
TB2.1 tests whether an agent can complete software tasks inside an isolated terminal environment, with each task’s verifier deciding success.
At the two edges, OpenCode reached 41.3% pass@1 at $0.71 list cost per attempt, while OpenClaw reached 20.7% at $1.82.
That gap compounds into the most useful result: $1.73 per solved task for OpenCode versus $8.80 for OpenClaw, a 5.1× difference with identical model weights.
Qwen Code provides another revealing comparison, nearly matching OpenCode at 40.0% while costing 1.95× more per attempt at $1.39.
The token data explains much of this cost spread: depending on the harness, average usage ranged from 1.78M to 5.12M input tokens per attempt while output averaged only 17k–36k.
Against the model’s 131k context window, that input equals roughly 14–39 complete windows sent during one attempt.
Output contributed only 3–4% of list-price cost, making repeated context the main economic variable.
Caching changes the absolute bill substantially: for the six harnesses with complete cache data, 96–98% of input was served from cache, reducing estimated cost by 5.5–6.4×.
The plot shows OpenCode’s $0.71 list-price estimate, while applying the measured cache discount lowers it to $0.13 per attempt, an 82% reduction.
Even after that adjustment, the central result holds, with pi and OpenCode still defining the Pareto frontier.
Together, these results suggest that context handling and cache use matter more economically than how much text the agent produces.
The benchmark contains 50 unique tasks with three repeated trials per task, so small pass-rate gaps should not be treated as definitive rankings.
Under the hood, the architecture separated benchmark execution from model serving: each Harbor attempt ran as an isolated Slurm CPU job, while Muse-Glimmer-30B inference stayed remote on Hugging Face Inference Providers through Together.
Harbor handled each harness’s lifecycle and collected its verifier result, while a shared wiring layer connected compatible harnesses directly and translated Anthropic Messages or OpenAI Responses into Chat Completions where required.
This separation also makes the setup reusable, because switching benchmarks mainly requires a new frozen split and task-image import while leaving the harness wiring unchanged.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Speculative Programmatic Tool Calling is such a neat and clean idea!
Most agent harnesses wait for the model to finish generating a REPL program before executing its tool calls. sPTC parses the program while it streams, pre-launches safe calls in a shadow REPL, and reuses the result if the final program makes that call. It can also parallelize independent calls that the generated code wrote as blocking. In effect, it is a small JIT layer for agent programs.
The first RLM experiments show up to roughly 1.2x speedups, depending heavily on the trajectory and tool latency.
Finally got around to reading this latest banger from @a1zhang. Follow him if you care about RLMs, agents, or harness design. He has a gift for making useful systems ideas feel obvious once you see them.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
AI Research Preference Models from FAIR sparked a lively discussion in the Hugging Face journal club yesterday!
The paper starts from the idea that AI agents have made proposing and implementing research ideas much cheaper: an agent can generate many plausible code changes or experiment plans quickly, but training and evaluating each one can still cost hours or days of scarce GPU time. That makes research taste—deciding which ideas are genuinely promising, which are redundant, and which are not worth pursuing—an increasingly important bottleneck; the authors call this research preference.
Their solution is a Research Preference Model (RPM), which sits between idea generation and expensive execution: the agent proposes several candidate experiments, then the RPM selects the one most likely to lead somewhere useful. An inference-only RPM inspects plans, code, and prior experiment results; an agentic RPM additionally runs small, cheap pilot experiments to gather evidence before choosing.
The broader intuition is similar to why frontier AI labs value exceptional researchers so highly: implementation capacity alone is not enough when there are countless things one could build; unusually good judgment about what to try, what evidence to trust, and where the hidden leverage is can determine how efficiently compute and teams translate into progress. The paper operationalizes a narrow, testable version of that judgment—ranking candidate ML experiments—and finds that it raises AIRS-Bench performance from 0.684 to 0.711 with reasoning alone and to 0.729 with pilot experiments, while reaching the baseline’s final result in roughly 15 rather than 24 hours.
It also has fun parallels to Monte Carlo Tree Search, my favorite algorithm :)
Worth a read:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HROFyrXbcAA9Og5.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool work by Sebastian Nagl, @matgrabmair and team!
BenGER is a benchmark for testing whether AI systems can solve German-law problems using the structured legal reasoning method taught in law school: identify the relevant rule, define its elements, apply the facts, and reach a conclusion. It includes 596 long, exam-style case tasks—581 from a public legal-education journal and 15 newly written Benchathon tasks—plus 531 shorter questions about legal principles. The Benchathon portion also contains 220 human-written answers, both unaided and written with optional AI assistance, allowing direct human–AI comparison.
Across 12 systems, closed flagship models like Gemini-3.1-Pro, Opus-4.7, and GPT-5.4 performed best, while the strongest open-weight model, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, was competitive with smaller closed systems but behind the flagships.
The clearest practical result is that people using AI scored 15.7 points higher out of 100 than people working without it, placing human–AI work roughly in the closed-flagship range. Their LLM-based grader correlated reasonably well with blind human graders (r=0.76), though the authors stress that the human-review sample is small and the judge should support human assessment and not replace it.
Worth a read:

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Same weights. $50 of harness search. 3x on Terminal-Bench.
We optimized the OpenCode harness for GPT-OSS-20B (high reasoning) with a
meta-harness: an agent that reads failures, patches the harness, and validates the improvement. The model never changed.
On held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1, the optimized harness scored 14.8%, up from
OpenCode's 4.8%. That is 3.08x, from $49.97 of API credits.
Three harness fixes carried most of the gain:
- i7, verify before stopping: the model often edited code and ended the session
without testing it. The harness gives it another turn to run the code.
- i14, continue announced actions: the model would say "now run X" and then stop. The harness keeps the session going so it runs X.
- i23, repair malformed tool calls: one extra `]` made OpenCode reject otherwise
valid commands. The harness repairs that clear-cut error.
How the meta-harness ran:
1. Start: stock OpenCode v1.18.13 + GPT-OSS-20B scored 8.5% on the dev split.
2. Iterate: Claude Code (Opus 5 max) reads the failed dev trajectories and proposes one patch. We build it and run it once per dev task, paired against the current parent.
3. Validate: candidates that clear a pre-registered margin get a 5-trial validation.
They become the new parent only if their validated score surpasses the current one.
4. Stop: the loop ended after 23 iterations and about 2.4k dev attempts, when the $50 search budget was spent.
Takeaway: pre-training puts capability in the weights, and post-training makes that capability usable. Harness optimization continues the same work at inference time, turning the model's behavior into more completed tasks. Same weights, 3x the finished tasks.

summary:
You can train your own Parity-aware BPE tokenizer in the HuggingFace library! See the docs for an example :)
Quoting @joelniklaus
Congrats to @clara__meister for getting the Parity-Aware BPE tokenizer merged into Hugging Face tokenizers!
Learn more about it here:
Use it like this:
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import ByteLevel
from tokenizers.trainers import ParityBpeTrainer
tokenizer = Tokenizer(BPE())
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = ByteLevel()
# Plain text files: one iterator per language
def lines(path):
with open(path) as f:
yield from f
trainer = ParityBpeTrainer(num_merges=32000, variant="base")
trainer.train_from_iterator(
tokenizer,
train_iterators=[lines("en.txt"), lines("de.txt"), lines("zh.txt")],
dev_iterators=[lines("en_dev.txt"), lines("de_dev.txt"), lines("zh_dev.txt")],
)

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Releasing LEXam-hard, a subset of the hardest open questions from LEXam.
LEXam is a bilingual legal reasoning benchmark built from 340 University of Zurich law exams covering Swiss, European and international law.
We scored all 2,541 open questions with the 16 open models from SwissLegalEvals, then defined difficulty as each question's mean score among the top seven models and kept the 546 below 50. DeepSeek V4 Flash screened that pool for questions that depended on missing material, dropping 52. Fable 5.1 reviewed those 52 and restored 24 that named the facts or public document they needed, leaving 518 questions.
Some low-scoring questions require a specific court decision, statute or scholarly position that the model does not know; we kept these because a legal research tool can help. We removed questions that referred to missing material, such as "see exercise 4.1" or "the above advertisement."
On LEXam-hard, Inkling leads at 40.8, down from 67.7 on the full set. Every one of the 16 models loses 9 to 30 points, and the spread between the best and worst model shrinks from 43 points to 25.
LEXam-hard concentrates the fifth of the exam where current open models have the most room to improve and legal research tools can matter.

clean_title: Synthetic pre-pretraining improves token efficiency at large scale
summary:
Prior work studied pre-pretraining (PPT) on small models and token budgets only. We scale it up to 7B parameters and 100B pretraining tokens across 4 data mixtures and 5 PPT tasks.
We conclude that PPT is beneficial at larger scale, saving at least 21B PT tokens at the 3B scale.
Listen to our paper to learn more:
Quoting @_gucciiiii
A last piece of my PhD work is out!
We ask whether "pre-pretraining" (PPT) (i.e., training on synthetic non-natural language data briefly prior to pre-training on natural language data) helps at scale.
This is the largest ever PPT study! (1/5)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTiDdgaW4AAUo4X.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTiDdgcWcAAV1PT.png
clean_summary:
Pre-pretraining (PPT) means training a language model briefly on synthetic, non-natural language data before the usual pretraining on natural language. Earlier studies looked at small models and limited token budgets, so it was unclear if PPT helps at larger scales.

Joël Niklaus and colleagues scale PPT up to 7 billion parameters and 100 billion tokens across multiple data mixtures and tasks. They find that PPT remains beneficial at this scale, saving at least 21 billion pretraining tokens for a 3 billion parameter model. This suggests PPT can improve training efficiency even for very large models.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Super excited to share that FinePhrase has been selected as an Oral Spotlight at #COLM2026!
I will present on Wednesday afternoon next week. First in Oral Session 4 at 3:30PM PT and then in Poster Session 4 between 4:30 and 6:30PM (Poster F-4-126).
If you're in SF, I am looking forward to seeing you at the talk or in the poster session!
What is FinePhrase all about?
Synthetic data is a standard component in training large language models, yet systematic comparisons across design dimensions, including rephrasing strategy, generator model, and source data, remain absent.
We conduct extensive controlled experiments, generating over one trillion tokens, to identify critical factors in rephrasing web text into synthetic pretraining data.
Our results reveal that structured output formats, such as tables, math problems, FAQs, and tutorials, consistently outperform both curated web baselines and prior synthetic methods.
Notably, increasing the size of the generator model beyond 1B parameters provides no additional benefit.
Our analysis also demonstrates that the selection of the original data used for mixing substantially influences performance.
By applying our findings, we develop FinePhrase, a 486-billion-token open dataset of rephrased web text.
We show that FinePhrase outperforms all existing synthetic data baselines while reducing generation costs by up to 30 times.
We provide the dataset, all prompts, and the generation framework to the research community.
Listen to the paper to learn more:

Joël Niklaus explains that the same model can behave very differently depending on the agent harness it runs in. title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
If you've used the same model in different harnesses, you've probably noticed it behaves very differently in each.
Our new technical deep dive shows how to fix this by training the model with RL inside the harnesses themselves:
In some cases, the gap is huge: before any training, LFM2.5-2.6B solved 62% of tasks in Mini-SWE-Agent but only 33% in Claude Code 😢
The obvious fix is to train inside the harness, but this isn't simple because the harness controls the agent loop, so the trainer never sees the exact tokens the model produced. We solved this with:
> a capture proxy in OpenEnv that records tokens + logprobs from harnesses
> @harborframework for the tasks and sandboxes
> TRL's super fast async GRPO trainer
Training LFM2.5-2.6B across four harnesses took it from 42% → 54% on held-out tasks, with gains in every harness and 31% fewer tool calls on tasks it already solved 🔥
Training in OpenCode alone mostly improved ... OpenCode 😅
Huge kudos to @adithya_s_k for leading this, and to @QGallouedec @DirhousssiAmine @SergioPaniego @ben_burtenshaw for enabling multi-harness training in TRL & OpenEnv!

Today, we're releasing the Carbon Annotation Database and the model behind it, Carbon-A.
We've used this model to discover 566.34 million new gene candidates across 22,617 species, thousands of which have never been studied like this before.
We wet-lab validated a number of these new genes in well-studied species, such as in cats, chicken, and arabidopsis (plant), with our partners at Active Site and @UCSD, with more extensive wet lab results on previously-unstudied genomes coming soon.
